skills.name: Find what is actually being asked
skills.definition: Read the last sentence of the problem before the rest of it. Contest problems routinely give you a natural quantity to find and then ask for something one step further - twice it, the number left over, the other one of the pair. Underlining the actual question costs five seconds.
recognizeWhen: how many more than the other
what is the value of twice the number
the question asks for the remaining ones
which of these is not true
misconceptions: I found the number I had been working towards and stopped, without checking what was asked.
I answered how many when the question said how many more.
I missed the word not in which of these is not true.

skills.name: Draw the diagram
skills.definition: When a problem describes a situation in words, drawing it converts memory work into looking. A rough sketch with the given numbers written on it is faster than re-reading the sentence four times, and it exposes relationships the words hide.
recognizeWhen: the problem describes positions in words
no picture is provided
he walks north and then turns east
the boxes are arranged in a row
misconceptions: I tried to hold the whole arrangement in my head instead of sketching it.
I drew the picture but did not label it with the numbers I was given.
I drew a picture that matched my first reading and never redrew it when that reading failed.

skills.name: Try small cases first
skills.definition: When a problem asks about a hundred of something, do two, three and four first. The small cases reveal the pattern or the reason, and they are cheap. This is the single most reliable way into a five-point problem you do not immediately see.
recognizeWhen: what happens with one hundred of them
the pattern continues for many steps
in general, how many are there
the problem uses a large number
misconceptions: I attacked the big case directly and got lost in the arithmetic.
I tried one small case, saw a pattern, and trusted it without a second case.
I chose small cases that were too special to show the general behaviour.

skills.name: Back-solve from the answer choices
skills.definition: The answer is one of the five given. Testing a choice is often much easier than solving forwards, especially when the forward route needs algebra. Start with the middle choice so that the result tells you which direction to move.
recognizeWhen: the answer choices are all numbers
which of these numbers satisfies the condition
solving forwards needs algebra you would rather avoid
checking a candidate is quick
misconceptions: I started testing at choice A and worked down, which took the longest possible time.
I found a choice that satisfied one condition and stopped without checking the others.
I back-solved even though checking one choice was harder than solving the problem.

skills.name: Eliminate impossible choices by bounding
skills.definition: Before calculating, ask how big the answer could possibly be and how small. Choices outside those bounds go immediately. Even when bounding does not name the answer, going from five choices to two changes what a guess is worth.
recognizeWhen: the answer must be less than the total
some choices are clearly too large
the answer has to be a whole number
it must be bigger than the part you can already see
misconceptions: I calculated exactly when two of the choices were obviously impossible.
I set a bound but then chose an answer outside it anyway.
I ruled out a choice using a bound I had not actually justified.

skills.name: Estimate to the nearest choice
skills.definition: When the five choices are far apart, a rough calculation picks the right one. Round aggressively, get an approximate answer, and choose the nearest. This is a decision about the answer choices, not a shortcut in the arithmetic.
recognizeWhen: the choices differ by a lot
which is closest to the true value
about how many
an exact calculation would take minutes
misconceptions: I rounded every number in the same direction and my estimate drifted too far.
I estimated but then picked a neat-looking choice rather than the nearest one.
I estimated on a question whose choices were close together.

skills.name: Spot the trick vs. decide to grind
skills.definition: Every five-point problem has a short way in, but you do not always find it. The skill is deciding, quickly and deliberately, whether to keep hunting for the idea or to start the long reliable calculation - and then committing to that decision.
recognizeWhen: there is probably a clever way to see this
the brute force route would take five minutes
the numbers are suspiciously convenient
you have been staring at it for a minute
misconceptions: I kept hunting for an elegant idea until the time ran out.
I started grinding immediately and missed a one-line observation.
I switched between the two approaches repeatedly and finished neither.

skills.name: Time triage: now, later, or guess
skills.definition: Seventy-five minutes across twenty-four or thirty questions means every problem gets a decision, not just an attempt: do it now, mark it and come back, or answer and move on. Made well, this is worth more points than any single piece of mathematics.
recognizeWhen: you are two minutes into a three-point question
the paper has questions you have not seen yet
this one looks long but doable
there are ten minutes left and five blanks
misconceptions: I spent eight minutes on question 22 and never saw questions 27 to 30.
I marked almost everything as later and ran out of time to return to any of it.
I kept going on a problem because I had already invested time in it.

skills.name: Never leave a blank - there is no penalty
skills.definition: Math Kangaroo takes nothing off for a wrong answer. A blank scores zero and a guess scores zero or more, so a blank is never the better choice. With one or two choices eliminated, a guess is worth real points across a whole paper.
recognizeWhen: you have no idea how to start
time is nearly up
you narrowed it down to two choices
there is no penalty for a wrong answer
misconceptions: I left the ones I could not do blank because guessing felt like cheating.
I ran out of time and did not fill in the remaining answers at all.
I thought a wrong answer would cost me marks.

skills.name: Check units and re-read before bubbling
skills.definition: Before committing an answer, spend three seconds on two questions: is this in the units they asked for, and is this the quantity they asked for. Most lost marks on questions a student can do are lost here.
recognizeWhen: the answer should be in minutes not hours
the choices are given in a different unit
you calculated the part but they wanted the whole
before you write the letter down
misconceptions: I gave the answer in centimetres when the choices were in metres.
I solved everything correctly and then wrote down the wrong letter.
I answered the question I expected rather than the one printed.

skills.name: Sanity-check with a second method
skills.definition: When time allows, confirm an answer a different way: estimate it, plug it back in, or count a small case by hand. A second method that agrees is worth far more than reading your first method again, because rereading repeats the same mistake.
recognizeWhen: you have spare time at the end
the answer came out surprisingly round
check by substituting the answer back in
does this answer make sense in the story
misconceptions: I checked by reading my working again and repeated the same slip.
I got a second answer that disagreed and picked the one I liked.
I skipped the check because the first answer matched one of the choices.

skills.name: Managing the 5-point block
skills.definition: The last third of the paper is worth 5 points a question and is where the paper is won or lost. Reaching it with time left, reading all of it before committing to any of it, and picking the two most tractable is a plan you make before the exam, not during it.
recognizeWhen: the last ten questions are worth five each
twenty minutes left and eight questions to go
some of the hard ones are easier than others
you have not read the final questions yet
misconceptions: I worked strictly in order and never reached the five-point questions I could have done.
I attacked the first five-point question I saw rather than the most tractable one.
I spent my remaining time on one hard question instead of two easier ones.

skills.name: Systematic listing
skills.definition: Write out the possibilities in an order that guarantees you cannot skip one or write one twice. Alphabetical, smallest first, or by a fixed rule - the order matters less than having one. This is the skill underneath almost every other counting skill.
recognizeWhen: how many different ways can
list all the possible outcomes
the numbers are small enough to write out
find every combination that works
misconceptions: I wrote the possibilities in whatever order they occurred to me and missed some.
I counted the same arrangement twice because I did not recognise it as one I had.
I stopped listing as soon as I had found a few, and assumed that was all of them.

skills.name: Tree diagrams
skills.definition: When a choice is followed by another choice, a tree shows every path through them. Each level is one decision, each branch is one option, and every complete path from top to bottom is one outcome. Counting the ends of the branches counts the outcomes.
recognizeWhen: first you pick one and then you pick another
how many outfits from these shirts and trousers
each step has a few options
draw all the ways this can happen
misconceptions: I drew branches for the first choice but only one branch for the second.
I counted the lines in the tree instead of the endings.
I let the number of second choices vary when it should have been the same for every branch.

skills.name: The multiplication principle
skills.definition: If one decision has 4 options and an independent decision has 3, together they have 12 outcomes. You multiply rather than add whenever the choices happen together rather than instead of each other. The word and usually means multiply; or usually means add.
recognizeWhen: how many ways to choose one of each
a code made of a letter then two digits
each position can be filled in several ways
how many different meals from the menu
misconceptions: I added the number of options instead of multiplying them.
I multiplied even though the two choices could not both happen.
I forgot that once an item is used it is no longer available for the next choice.

skills.name: Casework
skills.definition: Split the problem into a few situations that do not overlap and together cover everything, solve each one, then add. The two dangers are cases that overlap, which double-counts, and cases that leave a gap, which undercounts.
recognizeWhen: it depends on whether the first one is
consider the cases separately
either this happens or that happens
count them by size, largest first
misconceptions: I split the problem into cases that overlapped, so I counted some possibilities twice.
I forgot one case entirely and my total came out too small.
I solved each case correctly and then forgot to add them together.

skills.name: Arrangements of a few objects
skills.definition: When order matters, arranging n distinct objects gives n times n minus one times n minus two and so on. Three books on a shelf can be ordered six ways. Contest problems keep n small, so you can also list them - and listing is a good check.
recognizeWhen: in how many orders can they line up
how many different three-letter codes
the order they finish in matters
seat them around a table
misconceptions: I treated two arrangements as the same when the order was actually different.
I multiplied by the same number each time instead of counting down.
I forgot that swapping two identical objects does not make a new arrangement.

skills.name: Selections of a few objects
skills.definition: When order does not matter, count the ordered versions and then divide by the number of orders you counted each group in. Choosing two people from five gives ten pairs, not twenty, because each pair was counted in both orders.
recognizeWhen: how many ways to choose a team of
pick two of them, order does not matter
how many pairs can be formed
select a committee from the group
misconceptions: I counted the pairs as if order mattered, so I doubled every answer.
I divided by the wrong number when correcting for order.
I used arrangements because the word choose was not in the question.

skills.name: Counting paths on a grid
skills.definition: When you may only move right and down, the number of routes to a point is the number of routes to the square above plus the number to the square on the left. Writing that number into every square fills the grid and the corner holds the answer.
recognizeWhen: how many shortest routes from A to B
you may only move right or down
count the ways through the street grid
the ant walks along the edges
misconceptions: I counted routes that went backwards, which are not shortest routes.
I multiplied the width by the height instead of building the grid up square by square.
I forgot that a blocked square makes every route through it impossible.

skills.name: Handshakes and pairs
skills.definition: If everyone in a group of n shakes hands with everyone else, each person shakes n minus one hands, but every handshake involves two people, so the total is half of n times n minus one. The same shape counts games in a round robin and lines between points.
recognizeWhen: everyone shakes hands with everyone else
each team plays every other team once
how many lines join these points
how many pairs can be made from the group
misconceptions: I multiplied the number of people by the number of handshakes each and forgot to halve it.
I counted a person shaking their own hand.
I used the total number of people where I needed one fewer.

skills.name: Complementary counting
skills.definition: Sometimes counting what you do not want is far easier than counting what you do. Count everything, count the bad ones, subtract. Any question with the words at least or not is a candidate.
recognizeWhen: how many have at least one
how many do not contain
count the ones that fail and subtract
in how many ways can it not happen
misconceptions: I counted the bad ones and gave that as my answer without subtracting.
I subtracted from the wrong total.
I counted at least one as meaning exactly one.

skills.name: Inclusion–exclusion with two sets
skills.definition: When two groups overlap, adding their sizes counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once. A picture of two overlapping circles with the middle filled in first turns almost every one of these problems into arithmetic.
recognizeWhen: some students take both subjects
how many take at least one of the two
twelve like apples, nine like pears, four like both
the two circles overlap in the middle
misconceptions: I added the two groups and forgot that the people in both got counted twice.
I filled in the outer parts of the diagram before the overlap.
I thought both meant one group or the other but not both.

skills.name: Counting with restrictions
skills.definition: A rule like these two cannot sit together changes the count. Two reliable moves: place the restricted objects first and fill in around them, or count everything and subtract the arrangements that break the rule.
recognizeWhen: they must not sit next to each other
the first digit cannot be zero
the two friends insist on being together
no two of the same colour may touch
misconceptions: I counted every arrangement and forgot to remove the ones that break the rule.
I placed the free objects first and then found the restricted ones would not fit.
I treated the pair that must stay together as two separate objects.

skills.name: Counting by position (sliding window)
skills.definition: To count how many copies of a fixed shape fit inside a bigger one, count the positions its top-left corner can take rather than cutting the big shape into pieces. A two-by-two square fits into a three-by-three board in four positions, not one.
recognizeWhen: how many two by two squares are in this grid
count the rectangles of this size
how many ways can the tile be placed
the shape may overlap with itself in other positions
misconceptions: I cut the board into separate blocks instead of sliding the shape one step at a time.
I counted positions along one direction and forgot to do the same in the other direction.
I let the shape slide off the edge of the board.

skills.name: Counting shapes hidden inside a figure
skills.definition: A drawing of overlapping lines contains far more triangles or squares than the ones that are drawn as separate cells. Count by size - all the smallest first, then the ones made of four cells, and so on - so that no size gets forgotten.
recognizeWhen: how many triangles are in the picture
count all the squares of any size
the shapes overlap each other
how many rectangles can you find
misconceptions: I counted the squares I could see as separate cells and stopped there.
I found the small ones and the big one but missed the medium ones in between.
I counted the same shape twice from two different starting corners.

skills.name: Counting cubes in a stack, including hidden ones
skills.definition: A picture of a stack of cubes hides the ones behind and underneath. Counting layer by layer, or column by column across the base, reaches the cubes you cannot see. The question is usually how many cubes there are, or how many faces are painted.
recognizeWhen: how many small cubes make this solid
some cubes are hidden behind the others
the outside of the block is painted
how many cubes have exactly two red faces
misconceptions: I counted only the cubes I could see in the drawing.
I assumed the stack was solid when the picture showed gaps.
I counted the painted faces instead of the cubes that have them.

skills.name: Counting up to symmetry
skills.definition: When two arrangements are the same after turning or flipping the object, they should be counted once. Colouring the faces of a cube or the beads of a bracelet needs you to decide first which movements count as making it the same object.
recognizeWhen: two colourings are the same if you can rotate one into the other
beads on a bracelet that can be turned over
how many different dice can be made
arrangements that look the same when rotated count once
misconceptions: I counted every colouring separately even though turning the cube gives the same one.
I divided by the number of rotations without checking that each arrangement really had that many.
I allowed flipping when the problem only allowed turning.

skills.name: Overcount, then correct
skills.definition: A deliberate strategy: count in a way that is easy but wrong, work out exactly how much it overcounts by, and divide or subtract. Naming the overcount precisely is the difficulty, not the arithmetic.
recognizeWhen: each one was counted more than once
count them as if order mattered and then adjust
every arrangement appears several times in my list
divide by the number of times each is repeated
misconceptions: I knew I had overcounted but guessed at the correction factor.
I assumed every item was overcounted the same number of times when some were not.
I subtracted the overcount when I should have divided by it.

skills.name: The pigeonhole principle
skills.definition: If you put more objects into fewer boxes than there are objects, some box holds at least two. It answers how many must I take to be sure questions, and it is about the worst case, not about luck.
recognizeWhen: how many must you pick to be certain
prove that two of them share something
socks of different colours in a dark drawer
at least two people have the same
misconceptions: I answered with the lucky case instead of the worst case.
I forgot to add one after filling every box once.
I picked the number of boxes as my answer instead of one more than that.

skills.name: Extremal / worst-case counting
skills.definition: Some questions ask for the largest or smallest number that can be arranged, or how many are needed to guarantee an outcome. You have to argue on both sides: build an example that achieves the number, and explain why nothing better is possible.
recognizeWhen: what is the largest number that can be placed
how many are needed to guarantee
at most how many can be chosen so that
find the best possible arrangement
misconceptions: I found an arrangement that worked and assumed it was the best one.
I showed the number was impossible to beat but never built an example reaching it.
I answered with the typical case rather than the extreme one.

skills.name: Perimeter and area of rectilinear shapes
skills.definition: Perimeter is the distance all the way round; area is how much surface is covered. For shapes made of rectangles you can cut the shape into rectangles, or count squares. The two are independent: two shapes with the same area can have very different perimeters.
recognizeWhen: find the perimeter of this L-shaped figure
how many squares does the shape cover
the shape is made of unit squares
which of these shapes has the largest area
misconceptions: I mixed up perimeter and area because both are just numbers about the shape.
I forgot to include the sides whose lengths were not written on the diagram.
I assumed a bigger perimeter meant a bigger area.

skills.name: Grid coordinates and lattice reasoning
skills.definition: Points on a grid can be named by how far across and how far up they sit. Once positions have numbers, distance, direction and repetition become arithmetic. Most grid problems are really about the difference between counting lines and counting spaces.
recognizeWhen: the point is three squares right and two up
give the coordinates of the corner
the grid is labelled along the edges
move along the lines of the grid
misconceptions: I counted the gridlines when I should have counted the squares between them.
I wrote the up number first and the across number second.
I started counting at one instead of at the origin.

skills.name: Area by dissection and rearrangement
skills.definition: Cutting a shape and sliding the pieces somewhere else does not change its area. That lets you turn an awkward shape into a rectangle whose area you can read off. The cut you choose is the whole idea.
recognizeWhen: the shaded pieces can be rearranged into a rectangle
cut the shape along the dotted line
two triangles fit together to make a square
the pieces are moved but not overlapped
misconceptions: I assumed rearranging the pieces changed the total area.
I cut the shape into pieces that did not actually fit back together.
I found the area of one piece and forgot there were several.

skills.name: Area by subtraction (shaded regions)
skills.definition: When a shaded region is what is left after removing something, find the whole and the removed part separately and subtract. Trying to measure the odd-shaped remainder directly is almost always the harder route.
recognizeWhen: find the area of the shaded region
a circle is cut out of the square
the white part is removed from the whole
what fraction of the figure is shaded
misconceptions: I tried to measure the shaded piece directly instead of subtracting.
I subtracted the wrong way round and got a negative area.
I forgot that the cut-out shape might overlap the edge of the big shape.

skills.name: Angles on lines, in triangles, in polygons
skills.definition: Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees, angles round a point add to 360, and the angles of a triangle add to 180. Almost every angle chase is those three facts applied in turn until the unknown is cornered.
recognizeWhen: find the marked angle in the diagram
the lines are parallel
how many degrees is the angle at the centre
the shape is a regular polygon
misconceptions: I assumed an angle was a right angle because it looked like one in the picture.
I used the triangle rule on a shape that was not a triangle.
I found an angle correctly but then reported the wrong one of the two at that point.

skills.name: Properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
skills.definition: Named shapes carry guaranteed facts: a rhombus has four equal sides, a parallelogram has equal opposite angles, an isosceles triangle has two equal base angles. Recognising the name hands you the facts; assuming facts the name does not guarantee is the trap.
recognizeWhen: the shape is a parallelogram
two sides of the triangle are equal
which of these is always true of a rectangle
the diagonals of the shape cross
misconceptions: I assumed a quadrilateral with equal sides had to have right angles.
I used the picture's proportions instead of the properties I was told.
I thought every rhombus was a square.

skills.name: Circles: radius, diameter, and touching circles
skills.definition: A circle is every point the same distance from the centre, so the radius is the fact everything else is built on. When circles touch, the distance between their centres is the sum of the radii - drawing that line is usually the move.
recognizeWhen: the circles touch each other
the radius of the small circle is
the circle fits exactly inside the square
find the distance between the two centres
misconceptions: I used the radius where the problem gave me the diameter.
I forgot to draw the line joining the two centres.
I assumed a circle inside a square touches the corners rather than the sides.

skills.name: Line and rotational symmetry
skills.definition: A shape has line symmetry if folding along a line makes the halves match, and rotational symmetry if turning it less than a full turn leaves it looking the same. Counting the lines of symmetry of a shape is a matter of trying each candidate fold, not eyeballing it.
recognizeWhen: how many lines of symmetry does the shape have
which of these figures looks the same upside down
fold the shape in half so the halves match
the pattern repeats when you turn it
misconceptions: I counted a diagonal as a line of symmetry for a rectangle.
I confused turning the shape with flipping it over.
I said a shape had no symmetry because I only checked the vertical fold.

skills.name: Reflections, rotations, translations
skills.definition: Three ways to move a shape without changing its size: slide it, turn it, or flip it. Only the flip reverses left and right, which is why a reflected letter looks wrong and a rotated one often does not.
recognizeWhen: the shape is reflected in the dashed line
turn the tile a quarter turn clockwise
which picture shows the shape after the move
the stamp prints a mirror image
misconceptions: I rotated the shape when the problem asked me to reflect it.
I turned it the wrong way because I did not check clockwise or anticlockwise.
I reflected the shape but kept the letters facing the original way.

skills.name: Nets and folding, 2D to 3D
skills.definition: A net is a flat shape that folds into a solid. The useful question is never what does it look like flat, but which faces end up opposite each other and which edges meet. Tracking one face and its neighbours as you fold is more reliable than imagining the whole thing at once.
recognizeWhen: which of these nets folds into a cube
when the net is folded, which face is opposite
the box is unfolded and laid flat
which pattern would be on the hidden face
misconceptions: I checked that the net had six squares and assumed that was enough.
I tried to picture the whole fold at once instead of tracking one face at a time.
I thought two squares next to each other in the net end up opposite each other.

skills.name: Dice and cube face relationships
skills.definition: On a standard die opposite faces add to seven, and on any cube the three faces meeting at a corner are mutually adjacent. Most dice problems are solved by naming which faces are opposite before worrying about what you can see.
recognizeWhen: opposite faces of the die add to seven
the dice are stacked on top of each other
what number is on the hidden face
the cube is rolled over onto its side
misconceptions: I assumed the faces I could see were opposite each other.
I forgot that a die rolling over changes which face is down.
I used the opposite-faces rule on a cube that was not a standard die.

skills.name: Views of a solid: top, front, side
skills.definition: A single drawing of a solid hides information, so problems give you two or three flat views instead. Each view tells you the maximum height along one direction; putting them together pins down the shape, or shows that several shapes fit.
recognizeWhen: here is the view from above and from the front
which solid matches all three views
draw what you would see looking down
the picture shows the shape from the side
misconceptions: I read the top view as showing how many cubes there are rather than where they are.
I assumed only one solid could match the given views.
I mixed up the front view and the side view.

skills.name: Building and counting with unit cubes
skills.definition: Solids made of identical small cubes can be counted layer by layer or column by column. The same structure supports questions about volume, about surface area, and about how many more cubes are needed to complete a larger cube.
recognizeWhen: the solid is built from unit cubes
how many more cubes are needed to fill the box
the block is three by three by three
count the cubes in each layer
misconceptions: I counted the cubes on the surface and treated that as the total.
I multiplied the three dimensions when the solid was not a full rectangular block.
I forgot that removing a cube from inside does not change the outside view.

skills.name: Tiling and tessellation
skills.definition: A tiling covers a region with copies of a shape, no gaps and no overlaps. Questions ask how many tiles fit, whether a given shape can tile at all, or what the pattern looks like further along. Area gives a quick necessary check but never a sufficient one.
recognizeWhen: cover the floor with these tiles
the pattern continues in all directions
can the shape be tiled without gaps
how many tiles are needed to cover
misconceptions: I divided the areas and assumed the tiles would therefore fit.
I forgot that the tiles could be rotated.
I allowed tiles to hang over the edge of the region.

skills.name: Paper folding and hole punching
skills.definition: Fold a sheet, punch a hole, unfold: each fold doubles the holes and places them as mirror images across the fold line. Working backwards fold by fold, in the reverse order of the folding, is the only reliable method.
recognizeWhen: the paper is folded twice and then punched
what does the sheet look like when unfolded
a hole is cut through all the layers
the corner is folded over before cutting
misconceptions: I unfolded all the folds at once instead of one at a time in reverse order.
I doubled the number of holes but put them in the wrong places.
I forgot that a hole on the fold line does not double.

skills.name: Scaling and similar figures
skills.definition: Enlarging a shape by a factor multiplies every length by that factor, the area by the factor squared, and the volume by the factor cubed. Almost every mistake here is applying the length factor to an area or a volume.
recognizeWhen: the model is a scale copy of the real thing
each side is twice as long
the two shapes are similar
how many times bigger is the area
misconceptions: I doubled the sides and said the area doubled too.
I used the area scale factor on a length.
I assumed two shapes were similar because they had the same name.

skills.name: Shortest paths on and around shapes
skills.definition: The shortest route across the surface of a box is a straight line once you unfold the box flat. Around an obstacle, the shortest path hugs the corners. Both cases turn a curved or folded question into a straight-line one.
recognizeWhen: the ant crawls across the surface of the box
find the shortest route from corner to corner
the string is stretched tight around the shape
the path must go around the obstacle
misconceptions: I measured the route along the edges instead of unfolding the box flat.
I unfolded the box but chose a fold that was not the shortest one.
I assumed the straight line through the inside of the solid was allowed.

skills.name: Clock geometry: hands, angles, times
skills.definition: The minute hand sweeps 6 degrees a minute and the hour hand 0.5 degrees a minute, so the angle between them changes steadily and repeats. Nearly every clock problem is either an angle at a given moment, or a moment when the angle takes a given value.
recognizeWhen: what angle is between the hands at
the clock is reflected in a mirror
how many times a day do the hands overlap
how many minutes until the hands line up
misconceptions: I forgot that the hour hand keeps moving between the numbers.
I found one time when the hands line up and forgot it happens repeatedly.
I measured the angle the wrong way round the clock face.

skills.name: Reading a logical statement precisely
skills.definition: Contest logic turns on small words. All, some, none, only, at least and exactly mean different things, and the opposite of all are red is not none are red but at least one is not red. Reading the sentence twice is a mathematical step.
recognizeWhen: at least one of them is telling the truth
which statement must be true
all of the boxes contain
only one of these is correct
misconceptions: I read some as meaning not all, so I ruled out the case where every one worked.
I took the opposite of all are red to be none are red.
I answered with a statement that could be true instead of one that must be true.

skills.name: Truth-tellers and liars
skills.definition: Some speakers always tell the truth and some always lie. The method is to assume one speaker is truthful, follow the consequences all the way, and see whether anything contradicts. If it does, that assumption was wrong, which is itself information.
recognizeWhen: knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie
one of them is lying
each child makes one statement
how many of them are telling the truth
misconceptions: I assumed a speaker was truthful and stopped as soon as things looked consistent, without checking the rest.
I forgot that a liar's statement being false tells me something definite.
I tried to reason about all the speakers at once instead of assuming one and following it through.

skills.name: Elimination grids
skills.definition: When several items must be matched one-to-one, a grid with a cross for impossible and a tick for certain does the bookkeeping. Every tick immediately crosses out the rest of that row and column, which is where most of the progress comes from.
recognizeWhen: match each person to their pet
no two of them chose the same
work out who lives in which house
each one has a different favourite
misconceptions: I filled in a tick but forgot to cross out the rest of that row and column.
I tried to hold all the clues in my head instead of drawing the grid.
I used a clue once and did not come back to it after learning something new.

skills.name: Ordering and ranking from clues
skills.definition: Clues like A is taller than B but shorter than C pin down an order. Drawing a single line and placing people on it as clues arrive keeps the relationships visible, and shows clearly when the order is still not fully determined.
recognizeWhen: who finished third in the race
she is taller than him but shorter than
put them in order from oldest to youngest
the blue box is somewhere to the left of the red one
misconceptions: I assumed the order was fully determined when two people could still swap.
I read taller than as meaning immediately taller than, with nobody in between.
I built the order from the clues in the order they were given instead of starting with the most restrictive one.

skills.name: Parity arguments
skills.definition: Some things are impossible because an odd or even count can never change into the other. If every move flips two lights at once, the number switched on always changes by an even amount, so an odd target is unreachable. Parity proves impossibility, which counting never can.
recognizeWhen: show that this is impossible
each move changes two of them at once
can the counters ever all be face up
the pieces must be covered in pairs
misconceptions: I tried more and more examples instead of asking what never changes.
I found that parity was preserved but did not check the starting and target parities differ.
I claimed something was impossible when my move actually could change the parity.

skills.name: Invariants and monovariants
skills.definition: An invariant is a quantity that no allowed move ever changes; a monovariant only ever moves one way. Finding one turns an endless search into a one-line argument about what states can ever be reached, or about why a process has to stop.
recognizeWhen: whatever moves you make, this stays the same
prove the process must end
the total never changes
can you reach this arrangement from that one
misconceptions: I looked for a pattern in the examples instead of a quantity that never changes.
I found something that usually stayed the same but not for every allowed move.
I used a monovariant to prove impossibility when it only proves the process stops.

skills.name: Coloring arguments
skills.definition: Colour the board like a chessboard, or in stripes, so that every placed piece must cover a fixed mixture of colours. Counting the colours then shows immediately when a covering is impossible. The art is choosing the colouring.
recognizeWhen: can the board be covered by dominoes
two opposite corners are removed
each piece covers one of each colour
colour the squares like a chessboard
misconceptions: I tried to find a covering by trial and error rather than counting colours.
I chose a colouring that did not force each piece to cover a fixed mix.
I counted the colours correctly but forgot the pieces could be rotated.

skills.name: Working backwards
skills.definition: When you know how something ended and want to know how it started, run the steps in reverse and undo each one. Doubling becomes halving, adding becomes subtracting, and the order of the steps reverses too.
recognizeWhen: he had six left at the end
half of what remained was given away
what number did she start with
the process is repeated three times
misconceptions: I reversed each operation but kept the steps in their original order.
I undid took half by subtracting a half instead of doubling.
I worked forwards with a guess and gave up when it did not land exactly.

skills.name: Informal proof by contradiction
skills.definition: Assume the thing you doubt is true, follow it honestly, and arrive at something that cannot be. That rules the assumption out. In a multiple-choice contest it is usually used to knock out choices rather than to write a proof.
recognizeWhen: show that no such number exists
prove that it cannot be done
suppose there were such an arrangement
explain why this is impossible
misconceptions: I found no example and concluded none exists, without any argument.
I reached a contradiction but from an extra assumption I had quietly added.
I proved the opposite of what I assumed and thought I was finished.

skills.name: Weighing and balance puzzles
skills.definition: A balance tells you three things: left is heavier, right is heavier, or they are equal. Each weighing therefore splits the possibilities into three groups, and a good weighing splits them as evenly as it can.
recognizeWhen: one of the coins is heavier than the others
using the balance only twice
the scales tip to the left
two apples weigh the same as three pears
misconceptions: I forgot that the balance being level is a useful third outcome.
I planned my second weighing before seeing the result of the first.
I split the coins into two groups instead of three.

skills.name: The extremal principle
skills.definition: Look at the largest, the smallest, or the leftmost object, because the extreme one often has no room to misbehave. Arguments that go nowhere in general frequently collapse in one line once you consider the extreme case.
recognizeWhen: consider the largest of the numbers
take the person standing furthest left
there must be a smallest one
look at the closest pair
misconceptions: I reasoned about a typical object instead of the extreme one.
I picked the largest object but did not use the fact that nothing is larger.
I assumed an extreme object exists when the collection could be infinite.

skills.name: Translating a sentence into an equation
skills.definition: Turning words into arithmetic means naming the unknown, then writing what the sentence says about it in symbols. Three more than twice a number is not the same as twice three more than a number, and the order the words arrive in is not always the order of the operations.
recognizeWhen: three more than twice a number
let the number of apples be
the total is fifteen altogether
how many did she have to begin with
misconceptions: I wrote the operations in the order the words appeared instead of the order they happen.
I never wrote down what my letter actually stood for and lost track of it.
I solved for the unknown I named instead of the quantity the question asked about.

skills.name: Bar models for part–whole
skills.definition: Drawing quantities as bars makes part and whole relationships visible without algebra. Equal parts get equal boxes, a difference shows as an extra piece sticking out, and the answer is usually read off once one box's value is known.
recognizeWhen: she has three times as many as he does
how many more does one have than the other
the two amounts together make
draw a picture to show the amounts
misconceptions: I drew the bars without keeping the equal parts the same size, so the picture lied to me.
I found the value of one part and reported that instead of the total.
I drew three times as many as one bar next to a bar of the same size.

skills.name: Rate, time, distance
skills.definition: Distance is speed times time, and the same triangle rearranges to give speed or time. The usual difficulty is not the formula but keeping units consistent and handling two travellers whose journeys start at different moments.
recognizeWhen: how long does the journey take
two trains leave at the same time
he walks at four kilometres an hour
what was the average speed for the whole trip
misconceptions: I averaged the two speeds instead of dividing total distance by total time.
I mixed minutes and hours in the same calculation.
I forgot that the second traveller set off later.

skills.name: Combined work rates
skills.definition: If one worker takes 6 hours and another takes 3, think in jobs per hour rather than hours per job: they do one sixth and one third of the job each hour, so together one half, so two hours. Adding the times instead of the rates is the standard error.
recognizeWhen: working together, how long would it take
one tap fills the tank in six hours
they can paint the fence in
how much of the job is done each hour
misconceptions: I added the two times together and then halved them.
I added the rates but then gave the rate as my answer instead of the time.
I forgot that one of the taps was emptying the tank rather than filling it.

skills.name: Age problems
skills.definition: Everybody ages at the same speed, so the difference between two ages never changes even though the ratio does. Writing ages now and ages then in two rows, and using the constant difference, solves almost all of these.
recognizeWhen: in five years he will be twice as old
how old is she now
three years ago their ages added to
the difference in their ages is
misconceptions: I added the same number of years to one person and forgot the other.
I assumed the ratio of their ages stays the same over time.
I answered with the age in five years when the question asked for the age now.

skills.name: Money and change
skills.definition: Working with coins and notes means adding amounts, giving change, and finding which combinations are possible. It is arithmetic with a constraint: some totals cannot be made with the coins available, and that is often the actual question.
recognizeWhen: how much change does she get
using only these coins
what is the smallest number of coins
he pays with a note and receives
misconceptions: I found the total cost and gave that as the change.
I used a coin that was not among the ones I was allowed.
I found a way to make the amount and assumed it used the fewest coins.

skills.name: Unit conversion
skills.definition: Changing between centimetres and metres, minutes and hours, or grams and kilograms means multiplying or dividing by the conversion factor. Deciding which of the two it is by asking should the number get bigger or smaller catches nearly every slip.
recognizeWhen: give your answer in metres
how many minutes is that
the lengths are given in different units
convert to the same units first
misconceptions: I multiplied when I should have divided and my answer was a hundred times too big.
I converted one of the two quantities and forgot the other.
I gave the answer in the units of the question rather than the units asked for.

skills.name: Mixtures and weighted averages
skills.definition: When two groups of different sizes are combined, the combined average sits closer to the larger group's average. You cannot average the averages; you have to work with totals, or weight each average by its group size.
recognizeWhen: the two classes are combined
a mixture of two kinds of nuts
the average of the whole group is
twice as many boys as girls
misconceptions: I averaged the two averages even though the groups were different sizes.
I used the number of groups as my weight instead of the size of each group.
I found the total but divided by the number of groups rather than the number of items.

skills.name: Reading tables, charts, and graphs
skills.definition: Getting information out of a chart means reading the axes and the key first, then the bars or points. Most errors here are not mathematical: they are reading the wrong row, missing that the scale goes up in fives, or ignoring the units in the title.
recognizeWhen: the graph shows the temperature each day
according to the table
which category had the most
how many more chose one than the other
misconceptions: I assumed each gridline on the scale was worth one.
I read the value from the wrong row of the table.
I answered how many rather than how many more.

skills.name: Multi-step arithmetic word problems
skills.definition: Some problems need three or four ordinary steps in the right order. The skill is planning the route before calculating - writing down what you need next - so that you do not solve a step you do not need or stop one step early.
recognizeWhen: she buys several items and then shares them
work out how many are left at the end
the answer needs more than one calculation
after doing this, how many remain
misconceptions: I did the calculations in the order the numbers appeared in the question.
I solved an intermediate step and gave that as my final answer.
I lost track of which number meant what halfway through.

skills.name: Place value and digit positions
skills.definition: A digit's value depends on where it sits in the number. The 4 in 47 means forty, while the 4 in 74 means four. Problems about digits ask about the symbols in each position, not about the size of the whole number.
recognizeWhen: the problem names the tens digit or the ones digit
two digits get swapped and you compare the new number
a digit is crossed out, moved, or added on the end
the problem describes a number by its digits instead of its value
misconceptions: I read 47 and 74 as the same number because they use the same digits.
I thought the tens digit of 305 was 3, because 3 is the tens-looking one.
I added the digits together when the question asked for the number.

skills.name: Digit-constraint puzzles
skills.definition: You are told rules about a number's digits - their sum, their order, which ones may repeat - and asked which numbers obey all of them. The work is listing the possibilities in an order that cannot skip one, then testing each rule against the list.
recognizeWhen: find the largest number whose digits add to something
all the digits must be different
the number reads the same forwards and backwards
how many three-digit numbers have this property
misconceptions: I found one number that worked and assumed it was the only one.
I wrote digits in any order and lost track of which ones I had already tried.
I forgot that the leading digit of a number cannot be zero.

skills.name: Parity of numbers (odd/even behavior)
skills.definition: Odd and even is a property that survives arithmetic in predictable ways: even plus even is even, odd plus odd is even, odd plus even is odd. You can often answer a question about a huge calculation just by tracking whether each piece is odd or even.
recognizeWhen: the answer choices are all odd or all even
the problem asks whether something is possible, not what it equals
you are adding a long list of odd numbers
objects are paired up two at a time
misconceptions: I thought that if I add enough odd numbers together the total stays odd.
I decided zero was odd because it does not look like a normal even number.
I actually computed the whole sum instead of just tracking odd and even.

skills.name: Divisibility rules: 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10
skills.definition: A short test on the digits tells you whether a number divides evenly, without doing the division. A number is divisible by 3 when its digits add to a multiple of 3, by 4 when its last two digits are, by 5 when it ends in 0 or 5, and by 9 when its digit sum is.
recognizeWhen: which of these numbers is divisible by
a number leaves no remainder when divided
find the missing digit that makes it a multiple of
the objects can be shared equally among a group
misconceptions: I tested divisibility by 6 by checking only that the number was even.
I added the digits to test for 3 but then checked the sum against 3 instead of asking if the sum is a multiple of 3.
I used the last digit to test for 4, but 4 needs the last two digits.

skills.name: Factors, multiples, LCM and GCD by listing
skills.definition: A factor divides a number exactly; a multiple is what you get counting up by it. When two cycles have to line up, you want the least common multiple; when something has to be shared into equal groups, you want the greatest common divisor. At contest sizes, listing works.
recognizeWhen: two things happen every few days and you want when they coincide
cut into equal pieces with none left over
the largest number that divides both
find the smallest number that both go into
misconceptions: I mixed up factors and multiples because both words mean something about dividing.
I multiplied the two numbers together instead of finding their least common multiple.
I forgot that a number is a factor of itself.

skills.name: Remainders and modular cycles
skills.definition: When you divide and something is left over, that leftover repeats on a cycle. If today is Tuesday, then 100 days from now depends only on the remainder of 100 divided by 7. Finding the cycle length and the position inside it answers questions about enormous numbers.
recognizeWhen: what day of the week will it be in many days
the pattern repeats every so many steps
what is left over when you divide
the beads or tiles repeat in a fixed order
misconceptions: I divided and used the quotient when the question wanted the leftover.
I counted the starting day as day one and shifted my whole answer by one.
I found the cycle length but then counted forward the full number instead of the remainder.

skills.name: Last-digit behavior of products and powers
skills.definition: The final digit of a product depends only on the final digits of what you multiplied. Powers of a fixed number therefore cycle through a short list of last digits, so you can name the last digit of something astronomically large without computing it.
recognizeWhen: what is the units digit of a huge power
the answer choices differ only in their last digit
a product of many numbers ends in how many zeros
multiply a long string of numbers together
misconceptions: I tried to actually calculate the whole power on paper and ran out of time.
I found the cycle of last digits but started counting the cycle at zero instead of one.
I thought the last digit of a sum works the same way as a product without checking.

skills.name: Clever regrouping (pair to round numbers)
skills.definition: A long sum is much easier if you reorder it so pieces combine into round numbers. Pairing the first with the last, or grouping terms that cancel, turns a page of arithmetic into a line of it. The point is choosing the grouping before you start adding.
recognizeWhen: add all the numbers from one to some total
a long chain of plus and minus signs
the numbers are chosen so that pairs make ten or one hundred
several fractions that look like they will cancel
misconceptions: I added left to right and made an arithmetic slip halfway through.
I paired the numbers up but then forgot to count how many pairs there were.
I noticed a middle number left over and included it in a pair anyway.

skills.name: Fractions of a quantity
skills.definition: Taking a fraction of an amount means splitting it into equal parts and keeping some of them. Two thirds of 12 is 8 because 12 splits into three fours and you keep two of them. The trouble is always keeping straight what the whole is.
recognizeWhen: half of what is left over
two thirds of the students chose
a fraction of a group is then split again
the rest of the pizza was shared
misconceptions: I took the fraction of the original amount when it meant a fraction of what remained.
I found one third and stopped, instead of taking the two thirds the question asked for.
I added the two fractions' bottom numbers together.

skills.name: Percentages and simple discounts
skills.definition: A percent is a fraction with a hundred underneath. Increasing by 20% and then decreasing by 20% does not return you to the start, because the second percentage is taken of a different number. Naming the whole each time is the whole skill.
recognizeWhen: the price is reduced by a percentage
increased and then decreased by the same percent
what percent of the total is
a discount is applied on top of another discount
misconceptions: I added the two percentages together instead of applying them one after the other.
I took the second percent of the original price instead of the reduced price.
I thought a 50% rise then a 50% fall would bring the price back to where it started.

skills.name: Ratio as parts of a whole
skills.definition: A ratio of 2 to 3 means the whole splits into five equal parts, two of one kind and three of the other. Once you find what one part is worth, everything else follows. Confusing a part with the whole is the classic way this goes wrong.
recognizeWhen: the ratio of red to blue is
for every three of one there are two of the other
share an amount in the ratio
the two groups are in proportion
misconceptions: I divided the total by 2 and by 3 separately instead of by the five parts.
I treated the ratio two to three as meaning two out of three.
I found the value of one part and then forgot to multiply it back up.

skills.name: Estimation and order of magnitude
skills.definition: Sometimes the answer choices are far enough apart that a rough calculation is enough. Rounding each number to something friendly and asking roughly how big the answer should be is faster than exact arithmetic and it catches mistakes that exact arithmetic hides.
recognizeWhen: the answer choices are wildly different sizes
about how many would fit
roughly how long would it take
which of these is closest to
misconceptions: I rounded every number up and my estimate drifted far above the truth.
I did the exact calculation, ran out of time, and left the question blank.
I estimated but then picked a choice that was not actually the nearest one.

skills.name: Number lines and betweenness
skills.definition: A number line puts numbers in order and shows how far apart they are. Reading one means working out what each tick mark is worth first, then locating the value. Questions ask which number sits between two others, or what a marked point must be.
recognizeWhen: a point is marked on the number line
which number is between these two
the arrow points somewhere along the scale
put these numbers in order from smallest
misconceptions: I assumed each tick mark was worth one without checking the scale.
I counted the tick marks instead of the spaces between them.
I ordered negative numbers as if the bigger digit meant the bigger number.

skills.name: Operation puzzles and cryptarithms
skills.definition: Letters or shapes stand in for digits and you must recover which is which. Progress comes from the columns that are most constrained - a carry that must happen, a leading digit that cannot be zero - not from guessing at the first column you see.
recognizeWhen: each letter stands for a different digit
fill in the missing digits of this addition
put plus and minus signs between the numbers
the same shape means the same number
misconceptions: I started at the leftmost column instead of the one with the fewest possibilities.
I forgot that a carry from the column to the right changes what this column can be.
I let two different letters stand for the same digit.

skills.name: Means, and working backwards from a mean
skills.definition: The mean is the total shared equally. That makes it reversible: if you know the mean and how many things there are, you know the total, and a missing value is whatever makes the total come out right. Most contest questions use the mean backwards, not forwards.
recognizeWhen: the average of the five numbers is
what score is needed on the last test
the average went up when one more was added
find the number that was removed
misconceptions: I averaged the averages of two groups of different sizes.
I found the total but then divided by the wrong count.
I thought adding a number equal to the mean would change the mean.

skills.name: Continuing a visual pattern
skills.definition: A row of pictures follows a rule and you must say what comes next. The reliable move is to describe the change from each picture to the next in words before choosing, because a pattern that looks obvious often changes two things at once.
recognizeWhen: what comes next in the sequence
the pictures follow a rule
which shape continues the pattern
the design repeats along the strip
misconceptions: I looked at the pictures as a whole and guessed rather than naming what changes.
I spotted one thing that changes and missed a second thing changing at the same time.
I continued the pattern one step too few or one too many.

skills.name: Arithmetic sequences and the nth term
skills.definition: When a sequence goes up by the same amount every time, the nth term is the first term plus that amount repeated one fewer time than n. The off-by-one in that sentence is where nearly every mistake lives.
recognizeWhen: the numbers go up by four each time
what is the hundredth term
how many terms are there between
each row has three more than the one before
misconceptions: I multiplied the step by n instead of by n minus one.
I counted the number of terms as the difference between the first and last positions.
I found the rule from two terms without checking it on a third.

skills.name: Repeating cycles and position mod n
skills.definition: When a pattern repeats every few steps, the item at position 100 is determined by the remainder of 100 divided by the cycle length. Finding the cycle length and being careful about whether counting starts at zero or one is the whole job.
recognizeWhen: the beads repeat red green blue
what colour is the fiftieth one
the pattern repeats every six steps
which letter is in position one hundred
misconceptions: I divided by the cycle length and used the quotient instead of the remainder.
I got a remainder of zero and thought the answer was the first item rather than the last.
I counted the cycle length wrong by including the repeated first item twice.

skills.name: Growth patterns and figurate numbers
skills.definition: Some patterns grow by an increasing amount: a triangle of dots gains a longer row each time, a square gains an L-shaped border. Recognising the shape of the growth lets you jump to a distant term instead of drawing every stage.
recognizeWhen: each stage adds a row of dots
how many tiles in the tenth pattern
the border grows around the square
the differences between terms grow by one each time
misconceptions: I assumed the sequence went up by the same amount each time when the step itself was growing.
I drew the stages one by one and ran out of time before reaching the one asked for.
I found the number added at stage ten instead of the total at stage ten.

skills.name: Recursive rules
skills.definition: A recursive rule says how to get the next term from the ones before it, without giving a formula. To answer, you generate terms until you reach the one asked for, or until the sequence starts repeating.
recognizeWhen: each term is the sum of the two before it
the next number is double the last one minus three
start with two and apply the rule repeatedly
the sequence eventually repeats
misconceptions: I looked for a single formula when the rule was meant to be applied step by step.
I made an arithmetic slip early and every later term was wrong.
I did not notice that the sequence had started repeating.

skills.name: Patterns in tables and grids
skills.definition: Numbers arranged in a grid usually follow one rule across the rows and another down the columns. Finding both, and checking them against a cell you have not used, locates any entry without filling in the whole table.
recognizeWhen: the numbers are arranged in a table
each row follows the same rule
what number goes in the shaded cell
the grid is filled in a spiral
misconceptions: I found the row rule and assumed the column rule was the same.
I filled in every cell one at a time instead of finding the rule.
I checked my rule only on the cells I used to find it.

skills.name: Inferring a rule from examples
skills.definition: You are shown a few inputs and their outputs and must work out the machine in the middle. Several rules can fit a few examples, so the test of a candidate rule is whether it explains every example given, including the awkward one.
recognizeWhen: the machine turns three into seven
work out the rule and apply it
here are some examples of the operation
which rule fits all of these
misconceptions: I found a rule that fitted the first two examples and never checked the third.
I chose the simplest rule instead of the one that fits every case.
I applied the rule backwards when the question asked for the input.

problems.statement: Which number is exactly halfway between 10 and 20?

choices.misconception: I found half the gap but forgot to count it on from 10.
I gave the gap between 10 and 20 instead of the middle.
I counted the half-gap of 5 on from 20 instead of from 10.
I added the two numbers together instead of finding the middle.

hints: Count up from 10 and down from 20 at the same time.
The middle number is the same distance from both ends. Step up from the smaller number and down from the larger number together until you meet.
10 and 20 are ten apart, so the middle is five steps from each one.

solutions.reliable: The gap from 10 to 20 is ten, so halfway is five steps from each end, which is 15. The idea to keep: halfway means the same distance from both ends, so count from both sides and meet in the middle.

problems.whyOnTest: Finding a middle number is the start of understanding number lines, and adding the two ends is the mistake that comes first.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which one of these numbers is even: 7, 13, 18, 21 or 35?

choices.misconception: I split 7 into two piles, 3 and 4, and forgot the piles have to be the same size.
I added the digits, 1 + 3 = 4, and checked whether 4 was even instead of looking at the last digit.
I saw the 2 at the front and used that digit instead of the last one.
I thought every number ending in 5 could be shared out equally.

hints: Even numbers can be split into two equal piles.
Look only at the last digit. A number is even when it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, no matter how big the rest of the number is.
Try to share each number into two equal piles. Only one of them works.

solutions.reliable: A number is even when it can be shared into two equal piles, and that depends only on the last digit. Of these, only 18 ends in an even digit. The idea to keep: the last digit decides, so the front of the number can be ignored.

problems.whyOnTest: Looking at the wrong digit is the most common early mistake with odd and even, and two choices are built from exactly that.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square has sides of 3 cm. What is the distance all the way round it?

choices.misconception: I gave the length of one side instead of the way round.
I counted the sides instead of adding their lengths.
I added only two of the four sides.
I multiplied 3 by 3, which gives the space inside, not the way round.

hints: A square has four sides, all the same.
Walk round the shape in your head and add a side each time you turn a corner. Count the corners to be sure you have added four sides.
3 + 3 + 3 + 3, one for each side of the square.

solutions.reliable: A square has four equal sides, so the way round is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 cm. The idea to keep: count the sides first, then add one length for each, so none is missed and none is counted twice.

problems.whyOnTest: Losing a side while going round is the usual slip, and the choices for two and three sides are both here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ella has three 5-cent coins. How much money does she have?

choices.misconception: I added the 3 and the 5 instead of counting three coins.
I counted only two of the three coins.
I counted four coins instead of three.
I wrote the two numbers next to each other instead of adding the coins.

hints: Count on in fives, once for each coin.
Each coin is worth five, so count five, then ten, and keep going until you have counted one number for each coin you have. Then stop.
5, then 10, then 15, one count for each of the three coins.

solutions.reliable: Counting in fives for three coins gives 5, 10, 15 cents. The idea to keep: when every coin is worth the same, count on by that amount and make one count for each coin.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding the number of coins to the value of a coin is the standard mix-up, and it is the first choice here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pattern repeats: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, and so on. What colour is the tenth one?

choices.misconception: I counted in twos, as if the pattern were red, blue, so every even place looked blue.
I picked a colour that is not in the pattern at all.
I was not sure, so I chose both colours instead of following the pattern.
I thought the pattern stopped after the six colours written down.

hints: The pattern comes back to the start every three colours.
Write out the colours in groups of three. The tenth one begins a new group, so it is the same as the first colour in every group.
Colours 1, 4, 7 and 10 are all the first colour of a group.

solutions.reliable: The pattern repeats in blocks of three, so colours 1, 4, 7 and 10 are all the first in their block, which is red. The idea to keep: find how long the repeat is, then count in blocks of that size instead of one at a time.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting a repeating pattern in blocks instead of one at a time is the first real pattern skill, and guessing the commonest colour is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Half of the 12 apples in a basket are green. How many apples are green?

choices.misconception: I shared the apples into four piles instead of two.
I shared the apples into three piles instead of two.
I took two apples away rather than sharing them into two equal groups.
I doubled the apples instead of halving them.

hints: Share the apples into two equal piles.
Half means two equal piles with nothing left over. Deal the apples out one to each pile in turn, then count what is in one pile.
Two equal piles of apples from 12, and one pile is the answer.

solutions.reliable: Half of 12 means two equal piles, and 6 + 6 = 12, so each pile holds 6. The idea to keep: halving is sharing into two equal piles, which is why doubling the answer gets you back to where you started.

problems.whyOnTest: Halving and doubling are easy to swap round, and the doubled answer is on the list for exactly that reason.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the number 58, what does the 5 stand for?

choices.misconception: I read the 5 as counting single things rather than groups of ten.
I used the wrong size of group, since 58 is smaller than a hundred.
I used the other digit of the number instead of the 5.
I gave the whole number rather than what one of its digits stands for.

hints: In a two-digit number, the first digit counts tens.
Each place in a number stands for a different size of group. The digit on the right counts ones and the digit next to it counts tens, so read the position and not just the digit.
58 is 5 tens and 8 ones, which is 50 + 8.

solutions.reliable: 58 means 5 tens and 8 ones, so the 5 stands for 5 tens, or 50. The idea to keep: a digit's value comes from where it sits, not from the digit alone, which is why the same 5 means something different in 58 and in 85.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value is the base of everything else in arithmetic, and reading the digit without its position is the first error to fix.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the largest two-digit number you can make using the digits 4 and 9, each once?

choices.misconception: I put the digits in the order they were given rather than the order that makes a bigger number.
I used the 9 twice, but each digit can only be used once.
I used the 4 twice instead of using both digits.
I added the two digits instead of making a number from them.

hints: The first digit matters much more than the second.
To make a number as big as possible, put the larger digit where it counts for more. In a two-digit number that is the tens place, on the left.
Putting the 9 in the tens place makes 90 on its own, which already beats 49.

solutions.reliable: The tens digit counts for ten times as much as the ones digit, so the larger digit belongs on the left, giving 94. The idea to keep: to make a number large, fill the most valuable place first.

problems.whyOnTest: Ordering digits by place value is the point here, and keeping the digits in the order given is what most students do first.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana has 2 hats and 3 scarves. How many different hat-and-scarf pairs can she wear?

choices.misconception: I counted only the hats and forgot the scarves.
I counted only the scarves and forgot the hats.
I added the hats and the scarves instead of pairing them up.
I used three hats rather than two when making the pairs.

hints: Try every scarf with the first hat, then with the second.
Take one hat and count the pairs it can make with each scarf. Then do the same for the other hat. Adding those counts gives every pair exactly once.
The first hat makes 3 pairs and so does the second hat.

solutions.reliable: The first hat pairs with each of the 3 scarves, and so does the second hat, giving 3 + 3 = 6 pairs. The idea to keep: when two choices are made together, count the second choice once for every option of the first, which is why these counts multiply rather than add.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding instead of pairing is the error that this question is built around, and that answer is sitting in the list.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many lines can a square be folded along so that the two halves match exactly?

choices.misconception: I found the fold down the middle and stopped looking for others.
I found the two straight folds and missed the two corner-to-corner folds.
I found three folds and missed the fourth.
I counted each fold twice, once for each direction.

hints: Try folding sideways, downwards, and corner to corner.
Fold the square in every way you can think of: down the middle one way, the other way, and across each pair of opposite corners. Count only the folds where the halves match exactly.
Two folds go through the middle of the sides and two go through opposite corners.

solutions.reliable: A square matches itself when folded down the middle vertically, horizontally, and along each of its two diagonals, which is 4 folds. The idea to keep: look for folds through sides and through corners, because stopping at the obvious ones is how folds get missed.

problems.whyOnTest: Missing the diagonal folds is almost universal, and the answers for one, two and three folds are all offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Tom and Sara have 14 stickers altogether. Tom has 4 more than Sara. How many does Sara have?

choices.misconception: I used the difference of 4 as Sara's total instead of the gap between them.
I shared the stickers equally and ignored that Tom has more.
I gave Tom's total rather than Sara's.
I took 4 from 14 and gave the result without sharing what was left.

hints: Put Tom's extra four stickers to one side first.
Set the 4 extra stickers aside, so the two children would then have the same amount. Share what is left equally, and that gives the smaller total.
Setting 4 aside leaves 10 to share equally between the two.

solutions.reliable: Setting Tom's 4 extra stickers aside leaves 10 to split evenly, so Sara has 5 and Tom has 9, which checks against 14. The idea to keep: remove the difference first so the rest shares out equally, then put it back on the right person.

problems.whyOnTest: Splitting 14 in half is what a student does first, and that answer is on the list to catch it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is 3 + 5 + 7, and is the answer odd or even?

choices.misconception: I added correctly but thought three odd numbers would make an even total.
I added two of the numbers and then slipped by one on the third.
I added one too many while counting on.
I added only the last two numbers, 5 + 7, and left out the 3.

hints: Add two of them first, then the third.
Add the numbers in a convenient order, then check the total's last digit to decide odd or even. Doing the two steps separately keeps the adding mistake away from the odd-and-even decision.
3 + 7 = 10, which is easy to add 5 to, and the total ends in an odd digit.

solutions.reliable: Taking 3 + 7 = 10 first makes the total 15, and 15 ends in 5, so it is odd. The idea to keep: pair numbers that make a ten before adding the rest, then read odd or even off the last digit.
solutions.elegant: Three odd numbers always add to an odd total, so the odd part needs no adding at all.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding in a clever order and then checking parity are two separate skills, and the question needs both at once.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many different ways can three children line up one behind another?

choices.misconception: I counted the children rather than the orders they can stand in.
I multiplied three by three, which would let one child stand in two places.
I found four lines by trial and stopped before finding them all.
I thought there was only one way to make a line.

hints: Choose who goes first, then who goes next.
Decide the front of the line first: there are three choices. For each of those, two children are left for second place, and the last one has to go at the back.
Three choices for the front, then two for the middle, then one left over.

solutions.reliable: There are 3 choices for the front, then 2 for the middle, then 1 left, so 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 lines. The idea to keep: fill one place at a time and notice that each child used up is no longer available, which is why the count shrinks at each step.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing all six lines and getting a count that matches the reasoning is how this skill is learned, and most students stop at four.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sam starts at 30 and counts backwards in steps of 5. He does not say 30. What is the fourth number he says?

choices.misconception: I gave the first number I said rather than the fourth.
I stopped after only two steps.
I counted 30 as the first number I said, but the count starts after 30.
I counted one step too far and said five numbers.

hints: Say the numbers out loud and keep track with your fingers.
Count down in fives and raise a finger for each number you say, starting after 30. Stop when four fingers are up, rather than when the numbers run out.
25 is the first, then 20, then 15.

solutions.reliable: Counting down from 30 gives 25, 20, 15, 10, so the fourth number is 10. The idea to keep: the starting number is not one of the steps, so count the steps rather than the numbers you can see.

problems.whyOnTest: Whether the starting number counts as a step is the whole difficulty, and the three nearby answers are all off by one step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pencil costs 8 cents. Hana buys two and pays with a 20-cent coin. How much change does she get?

choices.misconception: I gave the price of one pencil instead of the change.
I subtracted the cost of one pencil from 20 and stopped.
I gave the cost of the two pencils rather than the change.
I added the money she paid to the cost instead of taking it away.

hints: Work out the cost of both pencils first.
Do the two steps in order: find the total cost of both pencils, then take that total away from the coin she handed over. Keep the two subtractions separate.
Two pencils cost 8 + 8 = 16 cents, and she paid 20.

solutions.reliable: Two pencils cost 8 + 8 = 16 cents, so the change from 20 is 20 - 16 = 4 cents. The idea to keep: in a two-step money question, total the cost before any subtracting, because subtracting one price at a time is where the steps get lost.

problems.whyOnTest: Change questions are two steps and the choices include the result of stopping after the first one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Using the digits 1, 2 and 3, each exactly once, how many different three-digit numbers can be made?

choices.misconception: I counted the digits rather than the numbers they can make.
I found four numbers by trying and stopped before finding them all.
I multiplied 3 x 3, giving three choices to only two of the places.
I let each of the three places hold any of the three digits.

hints: List them in order, smallest first.
Work through them in order so none is missed: start with the numbers beginning with 1, then those beginning with 2, then with 3. Each start gives the same small count.
Starting with 1 gives 123 and 132, and the same happens for each of the other two starts.

solutions.reliable: Each digit can lead, and the remaining two digits can go in either order, so each start gives 2 numbers and there are 3 x 2 = 6 in all: 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321. The idea to keep: list in a fixed order so nothing is missed, and count the pattern rather than trusting the list.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing without a system is how the 4 answer happens, and a fixed order is the habit the question is teaching.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi
