choices.misconception: I counted one diagonal from each corner and stopped there.
I counted three diagonals from each corner but forgot that each one gets counted from both ends.
I counted every line joining two corners, including the six sides.
I multiplied six corners by three diagonals each and never halved.

hints: Try a square first, then a pentagon.
Count the diagonals of a shape small enough to draw, then the next one up. The pattern in those counts is easier to trust than trying to see all the hexagon's at once.
A square has 2 diagonals, a pentagon 5, a hexagon 9. From each of 6 corners there are 3 diagonals, and each is counted twice: 6 x 3 / 2 = 9.

solutions.reliable: Start small. A square has 2 diagonals and a pentagon has 5 - both easy to draw and count. For the hexagon, each of the 6 corners joins to 3 others that are not its neighbours, giving 6 x 3 = 18 ends of diagonals. Every diagonal has two ends, so there are 18 divided by 2 = 9. Check against the small cases: the same reasoning gives 4 x 1 / 2 = 2 for a square and 5 x 2 / 2 = 5 for a pentagon, both correct. The transferable idea: build the rule on cases you can draw, then trust it on the one you cannot.
solutions.elegant: A shape with n corners has n(n - 3)/2 diagonals, giving 6 x 3 / 2 = 9.

problems.whyOnTest: Forgetting to halve is the same error as in the handshake count, and small cases are what let a student check the rule instead of hoping.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A shop sells pencils in packs of 4 and packs of 7. What is the largest number of pencils you cannot buy exactly?

choices.misconception: I found a number I could not make and stopped before checking the larger ones.
I saw 14, 15 and 16 could be made and stopped without checking 17.
I thought 21 could not be made because it is not a multiple of 4, forgetting three packs of 7.
I multiplied the two pack sizes, but that number is a multiple of both.

hints: Try every number in turn and mark the ones you can make.
Work upwards and mark each number you can build from fours and sevens. Once four numbers in a row can all be made, every larger number can too, because you can add another four.
Once 18, 19, 20 and 21 can all be made, adding fours reaches everything above.

solutions.reliable: Checking upwards, 17 cannot be made, but 18, 19, 20 and 21 all can, and from four consecutive makeable numbers you reach every larger one by adding fours. So 17 is the largest that fails. The transferable idea: four consecutive successes close the question, because the smaller pack size then carries you forever.
solutions.elegant: With packs of 4, you only ever need to find four consecutive makeable numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Trying small cases in order, and knowing when to stop, is the whole method, and the choices reward stopping early.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A clock loses 2 minutes every hour. It is set correctly at 8 am. What time does it show at 2 pm the same day?

choices.misconception: I counted seven hours by counting both 8 and 2, losing 14 minutes.
I counted five hours of loss rather than six.
I subtracted two minutes once rather than once for every hour.
I added the lost minutes instead of taking them away.

hints: Count the hours first, then the minutes lost.
Work out how many hours pass between the two times, multiply that by the loss per hour, and take the total loss away from the correct time. Keep the two steps apart.
Six hours pass from 8 am to 2 pm, and the clock loses 2 minutes in each.

solutions.reliable: From 8 am to 2 pm is 6 hours, so the clock loses 6 x 2 = 12 minutes and shows 1:48. The transferable idea: count the number of intervals before multiplying, because the loss happens once per hour and not once overall.

problems.whyOnTest: Losing count of the hours, or applying the loss only once, are the two standard errors and both are in the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three cats catch three mice in three minutes. How many cats are needed to catch 99 mice in 99 minutes?

choices.misconception: I thought each cat catches a mouse every minute, forgetting it took them three minutes.
I split the 99 minutes into three-minute blocks and used one cat per block.
I matched one cat to each mouse, ignoring that the time grew as well.
I multiplied the mice by the cats with no reasoning about the rate.

hints: Work out what one cat does in one minute.
Reduce the statement to a single cat over a single minute. Then scale that rate up to the time and the number of mice the question asks about, and see how many cats it needs.
Three cats in three minutes is one mouse per cat, so a cat catches a mouse every three minutes.

solutions.reliable: Three cats catching three mice in three minutes means each cat catches one mouse every three minutes. In 99 minutes one cat catches 33 mice, so three cats catch 99. The transferable idea: reduce to one worker and one unit of time before scaling, because the time grew by the same factor as the mice.
solutions.elegant: Both the mice and the minutes grew by the same factor, so the number of cats cannot change.

problems.whyOnTest: This is the classic question where scaling only one quantity gives a wrong answer, and three of the choices come from doing exactly that.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The digits 1, 2, 3 and 4 are each used once to make two two-digit numbers. What is the largest possible sum?

choices.misconception: I added the four digits as single numbers instead of making two-digit numbers.
I made two numbers from the digits but put the small ones in the tens places.
I made 43 and then added the 2 and the 1 as single digits instead of making a second two-digit number.
I built one large number and one small one rather than putting both large digits in the tens places.

hints: Think about which digits should sit in the tens places.
A digit in the tens place counts ten times as much, so the two largest digits belong there. The two smaller digits then fill the ones places, and their order does not change the sum.
Putting 4 and 3 in the tens places contributes 40 + 30 before the ones digits are added.

solutions.reliable: Tens digits count for ten times as much, so 4 and 3 belong there. That gives 40 + 30 = 70 from the tens, plus 1 + 2 = 3 from the ones, so the largest sum is 73, reached by 41 + 32 or 42 + 31. The transferable idea: put the largest digits where the place value is highest, and the order of the remaining digits then makes no difference.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value decides this, not trial and error, and the distractors are what trial produces.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a race, Ana finished ahead of Ben. Carl finished behind Ben but ahead of Dia. Emma finished ahead of Ana. Who finished third?

choices.misconception: I read the clue about Ana and Ben backwards, putting Emma and Ben in front of Ana.
I put the runners in the order their names appear in the clues, Ana, Ben, Carl, Dia, Emma, and forgot Emma belongs at the front.
I used only the clue about Ben, Carl and Dia and took the third name in it.
I placed Emma third rather than first, reading the last clue backwards.

hints: Join the clues into one line from front to back.
Write each clue as an arrow and link them where a runner appears twice. When all five sit on one chain, count positions from the front rather than from the middle.
Emma, then Ana, then Ben, then Carl, then Dia.

solutions.reliable: The clues chain as Emma, Ana, Ben, Carl, Dia, so third place is Ben. The transferable idea: build one chain before answering, and count from the front, because counting from whichever runner the clues mention first is how positions get misread.

problems.whyOnTest: Chaining clues into one order is the skill, and every distractor comes from counting from the wrong end or the wrong runner.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square sheet is folded in half, then in half the other way. The corner where the two folds meet is cut off. How many holes does the unfolded sheet have?

choices.misconception: I thought cutting a corner only trims an edge, but this corner is the middle of the sheet.
I assumed each fold doubled the number of holes without checking where the corner sits.
I multiplied by two for each fold, which counts cut pieces rather than holes.
I doubled three times, as though the paper had been folded three times.

hints: Work out which corner ends up at the centre of the paper.
Folding in half twice brings one corner of the folded square to the centre of the original sheet. Cutting that corner removes paper from the middle, and the layers all line up there.
The corner where the two fold lines meet is the centre of the unfolded sheet.

solutions.reliable: Two folds bring the centre of the original square to one corner of the folded shape. Cutting that corner removes paper from the middle of the sheet, and because the four layers coincide there, the result is a single hole. The transferable idea: find where each corner of the folded shape sits on the unfolded sheet before counting anything.
solutions.elegant: Cut the corner that the fold lines meet at, and all four layers are the same place on the sheet.

problems.whyOnTest: Paper folding is answered by tracking which corner is the centre, not by doubling for each fold, and the doubling answers are all offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana has some stickers. She gives half to Ben, then half of what is left to Carl, and has 5 stickers remaining. How many did she start with?

choices.misconception: I doubled once rather than twice, undoing only one of the two gifts.
I added five for each person rather than undoing the halving.
I got 20 and then added her 5 left over again, counting them twice.
I doubled three times rather than twice.

hints: Work backwards and undo each step.
Start from the five she has left and undo the steps in reverse order. Each gift was half of what she held, so undoing one means doubling, and there are two to undo.
Five left means ten before Carl, since Carl took half of what was there.

solutions.reliable: Working backwards, 5 left means 10 before Carl's half, and 10 means 20 before Ben's half. Checking forwards, 20 gives 10 to Ben, then 5 to Carl, leaving 5. The transferable idea: undo the steps in reverse order and then check forwards, since the forward check costs seconds and catches every slip.
solutions.elegant: Two halvings leave a quarter, so the start was four times what remains.

problems.whyOnTest: Doubling the wrong number of times is the usual error, and the choices include both one doubling too few and one too many.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many times does the digit 1 appear when all the numbers from 1 to 30 are written out?

choices.misconception: I counted only 1, 10 and 21, missing most of the teens.
I counted only the ten numbers from 10 to 19 and forgot 1, 21 and the second 1 in 11.
I counted the numbers containing a 1 rather than the times the digit appears.
I assumed one digit 1 for each number in the list.

hints: Count the ones place and the tens place separately.
Split the job: first count the numbers whose last digit is 1, then those whose tens digit is 1. Add the two counts, remembering that 11 is counted in both because it has two ones.
Last digit 1: 1, 11, 21. Tens digit 1: 10 up to 19.

solutions.reliable: Numbers ending in 1 are 1, 11 and 21, which is 3 ones. Numbers with 1 in the tens place are 10 to 19, which is another 10. Together that is 13, with 11 contributing one from each count. The transferable idea: count one digit position at a time, because a number with two ones must be counted twice.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting numbers rather than digit appearances is the standard error, and that answer is on the list.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five friends each give one present to each of the others. How many presents are given?

choices.misconception: I counted the presents one friend gives, not the whole group's.
I counted the friends rather than the presents.
I counted each pair once, but a present goes one way and both directions happen.
I let each friend give a present to themselves as well as the others.

hints: Each friend gives a present to four others.
Count from one friend's point of view: they give a present to everybody except themselves. Multiply by the number of friends, and do not divide, because a present has a giver and a receiver.
Each of the five gives four presents away.

solutions.reliable: Each of the 5 friends gives a present to the other 4, so 5 x 4 = 20 presents change hands. There is no halving here, because a present from A to B is different from one from B to A. The transferable idea: ask whether the direction matters, since handshakes halve and presents do not.

problems.whyOnTest: Presents and handshakes look identical in words and differ by a factor of two, and the halved answer is deliberately offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A number is doubled, then 6 is added, and the answer is 20. What was the number?

choices.misconception: I halved 20 first and then took away 6, undoing the steps in the wrong order.
I added 6 instead of taking it away, then halved 26.
I subtracted 6 and gave the result without halving.
I added 6 rather than taking it away.

hints: Undo the adding first, then the doubling.
The last thing done was adding 6, so undo that first by subtracting. Then undo the doubling by halving. Running the steps forwards on your answer is a free check.
20 - 6 = 14, and 14 came from doubling the number.

solutions.reliable: Undoing in reverse order, 20 - 6 = 14 and half of 14 is 7. Checking forwards, 7 doubled is 14 and 14 + 6 = 20. The transferable idea: undo operations in the opposite order to the one they were applied, because reversing the order is what produces the near-miss answers.
solutions.elegant: Testing the five choices forwards takes seconds and only one lands on 20.

problems.whyOnTest: Undoing out of order gives an answer that is close enough to look right, and it is on the list.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six identical books weigh the same as nine identical notebooks. How many notebooks weigh the same as four books?

choices.misconception: I matched one notebook to one book, ignoring the given weights.
I added the difference of three rather than scaling in proportion.
I doubled the four books, which is not the ratio given.
I reused the nine from the question without scaling it down.

hints: Find how many notebooks balance two books.
Simplify the given balance by dividing both sides by the same number, so that the book count becomes a factor of four. Then scale back up to four books.
Six books balance nine notebooks, so two books balance three notebooks.

solutions.reliable: Dividing the balance by three, 2 books weigh the same as 3 notebooks. Four books are two lots of that, so they balance 6 notebooks. The transferable idea: simplify a balance to its smallest whole-number form first, then scale once, rather than scaling a large ratio directly.

problems.whyOnTest: Simplifying the balance first makes this a single step, and adding the difference rather than scaling is the usual error.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the smallest number that is greater than 50 and divisible by 7?

choices.misconception: I gave the largest multiple of seven below fifty rather than above it.
I took the first number above 50 without checking it divides by 7.
I added seven to fifty, but fifty is not itself a multiple of seven.
I jumped to a multiple of ten rather than the next multiple of seven.

hints: Count up through the seven times table.
Say the seven times table out loud until you pass fifty, then take the first value past it. Adding seven to fifty does not work, because fifty is not in the table.
7 x 7 = 49, which is just under fifty.

solutions.reliable: The seven times table runs 42, 49, 56, so the first multiple above 50 is 56. The transferable idea: step through the times table rather than adding the divisor to the boundary, which only works when the boundary is itself a multiple.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding seven to fifty is the mistake almost everybody makes first, and that answer is on the list.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle is 7 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is the distance all the way around it?

choices.misconception: I added one length and one width and stopped.
I added the two lengths and forgot both widths.
I multiplied the two measurements, which gives the space inside instead.
I counted four sides of 7 cm rather than two of each measurement.

hints: A rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
Walk round the shape and add a side at every corner. There are four sides, with the two lengths equal to each other and the two widths equal to each other.
7 + 3 + 7 + 3, one for each side.

solutions.reliable: The way round is 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 cm. The transferable idea: a rectangle has two of each measurement, so add all four sides, and multiplying the two numbers answers a different question entirely.

problems.whyOnTest: Confusing the distance round with the space inside is the standard mix-up, and the multiplied answer is offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which number is three tens and twelve ones?

choices.misconception: I used only the 2 from the twelve ones and dropped the extra ten.
I wrote the digits next to each other instead of adding the groups.
I multiplied three by twelve instead of adding thirty and twelve.
I added the three and the twelve as plain numbers.

hints: Twelve ones is more than one ten.
Write the value of each part: three tens is 30, and twelve ones is 12. Add them as numbers rather than writing the digits next to each other.
30 + 12 is the number.

solutions.reliable: Three tens is 30 and twelve ones is 12, so the number is 42. The transferable idea: a digit's name and its value are different things, so convert each part to its value and add, which also handles the extra ten hidden inside twelve ones.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value breaks down when one part overflows its column, which is exactly what twelve ones does here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a normal die, opposite faces add to 7. The top face shows 2. What is on the bottom face?

choices.misconception: I assumed the opposite face matched the top face.
I used the largest face value rather than the one that completes the 7.
I gave the total of the two faces instead of the hidden one.
I added 2 to 7 instead of taking it away.

hints: The two faces must add to seven together.
The top and the bottom are an opposite pair, so their values add to 7. Subtract the face you can see from 7 to find the one you cannot.
7 - 2 gives the hidden face.

solutions.reliable: Opposite faces of a die add to 7, so the bottom face is 7 - 2 = 5. The transferable idea: a hidden face on a die is always found by subtracting the visible one from 7, and the same rule settles the other two pairs.

problems.whyOnTest: Giving the total rather than the hidden face is the usual slip, and the 7 is sitting in the choices for that reason.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is 25 + 38 + 75?

choices.misconception: I lost ten somewhere while carrying between the columns.
I added only the 30 from the 38 and forgot its 8 ones.
I gained ten while carrying between the columns.
I added the two numbers that make a hundred and stopped.

hints: Two of these numbers make a round hundred together.
Look for a pair that adds to a round number and do that pair first. Adding the third number to a round hundred is far easier than adding all three in the order given.
25 + 75 = 100, and then the 38 is added to that.

solutions.reliable: Taking 25 + 75 = 100 first leaves 100 + 38 = 138. The transferable idea: reorder an addition to make a round number first, because adding to a round hundred removes every chance of a carrying mistake.

problems.whyOnTest: Regrouping to a round number is the habit that makes mental arithmetic reliable, and both carrying slips are offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Today is Tuesday. What day of the week will it be in 100 days?

choices.misconception: I found the remainder 2 but counted the two days starting from today rather than starting from tomorrow.
I divided 100 by 7 and used the quotient of 14, treating the leftover days as if there were none.
I remembered there was a remainder but used a remainder of 1 instead of working it out.
I counted 100 divided by 7 as 14 remainder 3 instead of remainder 2.

hints: Days repeat every seven.
Only the remainder when you divide by 7 matters, because 7 days always brings you back to the same weekday. Work out that remainder and count that many days forward.
100 divided by 7 is 14 remainder 2. Fourteen whole weeks land back on Tuesday, and 2 more days is Thursday.

solutions.reliable: Weekdays repeat every 7 days, so divide 100 by 7: that is 14 remainder 2. The 14 whole weeks bring you back to Tuesday, and then 2 more days gives Wednesday, Thursday. The answer is Thursday. The transferable idea: with anything cyclic, throw away the whole cycles and keep only the remainder.

problems.whyOnTest: Calendar questions are remainder questions in disguise, and using the quotient instead of the remainder is the standard slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a triangle, one angle is 90 degrees and another is 35 degrees. What is the third angle?

choices.misconception: I assumed the triangle was isosceles because it had a right angle, so I repeated the 35.
I assumed a right-angled triangle always has two 45 degree angles.
I subtracted 35 from 100 instead of from 90, mixing the angle sum up with a round number.
I subtracted only the 35 from 180 and forgot to take off the right angle as well.

hints: The three angles add to 180 degrees.
Add the two angles you know, then subtract from the angle sum of a triangle. Nothing about the picture matters here beyond those two numbers.

solutions.reliable: The angles of any triangle add to 180 degrees. Two of them are 90 and 35, which come to 125. The third is 180 - 125 = 55 degrees. The transferable idea: in a right-angled triangle the two non-right angles always add to 90, which is a faster route to the same answer.
solutions.elegant: In a right-angled triangle the other two angles must add to 90, so the third is simply 90 - 35 = 55.

problems.whyOnTest: Angle chases start here, and assuming a right-angled triangle is also isosceles is the first wrong turn students take.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A password is one letter from A, B, C followed by two digits from 1 to 5. Digits may repeat. How many passwords are possible?

choices.misconception: I added the number of options at each step instead of multiplying them.
I treated the two digits as one choice of ten rather than two independent choices of five.
I assumed the two digits had to be different, so I used 5 times 4 for them.
I used 5 choices for the letter position as well, forgetting there are only three letters.

hints: Count the options at each position.
The three positions are chosen independently, so multiply the number of options at each one. Repeats are allowed, so the digit count does not shrink for the second digit.
3 letters times 5 digits times 5 digits = 75.

solutions.reliable: There are three independent positions. The letter has 3 options; the first digit has 5; the second digit also has 5, because repeats are allowed. Multiply: 3 x 5 x 5 = 75. The transferable idea: independent choices multiply, and repeats allowed means the count does not drop for later positions.

problems.whyOnTest: The multiplication principle is the backbone of contest counting, and adding instead of multiplying is the most common single error in the strand.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Red and blue counters are in the ratio 3 to 5. There are 40 counters altogether. How many are red?

choices.misconception: I found what one part is worth and gave that as my answer instead of multiplying it back up.
I divided 40 by the five blue parts instead of by the eight parts that make the whole.
I read the ratio 3 to 5 as meaning 3 out of every 5 and worked from that.
I found the value of one part correctly but then multiplied by 5 instead of 3, giving the blue counters.

hints: Add the parts of the ratio first.
A ratio of 3 to 5 splits the whole into 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts. Find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as the question asks for.
8 parts make 40, so one part is 5. Red is 3 parts, so 3 x 5 = 15.

solutions.reliable: The ratio 3 to 5 means the counters split into 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts. Since 8 parts make 40 counters, one part is 40 divided by 8 = 5. Red takes 3 parts, so there are 3 x 5 = 15 red counters. Check: blue is 5 x 5 = 25, and 15 + 25 = 40. The transferable idea: add the parts before you divide anything.

problems.whyOnTest: Ratio questions are lost by dividing by one side of the ratio rather than by the total number of parts.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four beads - one red, one green, one blue, one yellow - are threaded on a circular bracelet. Two bracelets are the same if one can be rotated into the other. How many different bracelets are there?

choices.misconception: I also treated bracelets that are mirror images as the same, but only rotations were allowed.
I divided the number of beads by itself rather than dividing the number of arrangements by the number of rotations.
I divided the 24 arrangements by 2 instead of by the 4 rotations of a circle of four beads.
I counted every arrangement in a line and forgot that rotating a bracelet gives the same bracelet.

hints: Count the arrangements first, then divide.
Count all the ways to place four different beads in four positions, then work out how many of those arrangements are just rotations of each other. Each bracelet appears once per rotation.
There are 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 arrangements in a line. A circle of four positions has 4 rotations, and every arrangement is counted once per rotation, so 24 divided by 4 = 6.

solutions.reliable: First count arrangements as if the positions were fixed: 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24. Now notice that rotating a bracelet by one, two or three positions gives the same bracelet, so each genuine bracelet has been counted 4 times. Divide: 24 divided by 4 = 6. The transferable idea: overcount deliberately, then divide by exactly how many times each object was counted.
solutions.elegant: Hold the red bead fixed and arrange the other three around it: 3 x 2 x 1 = 6, with no division needed.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting up to symmetry is a genuine 5-point idea, and it is the first place students meet a deliberate overcount-and-correct.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A jacket costs 80 euros. Its price is reduced by 25%. What is the new price?

choices.misconception: I worked out the size of the discount and gave that as the new price instead of subtracting it.
I treated a quarter off as half off and took the price down to 40.
I applied the 25% reduction twice, taking 80 down to 60 and then 60 down to 45.
I subtracted 25 euros rather than 25 percent, treating the percentage as an amount of money.

hints: A quarter off means three quarters left.
Either find 25% and subtract it, or find 75% of the price directly. The second route is one step and avoids reporting the discount as though it were the price.
25% of 80 is 20, so the new price is 80 - 20 = 60. Equivalently, 75% of 80 is 60.

solutions.reliable: 25% of 80 is 80 divided by 4, which is 20. Take that off the original price: 80 - 20 = 60 euros. The transferable idea: reducing by 25% is the same as keeping 75%, and computing what remains directly avoids reporting the discount by mistake.
solutions.elegant: Keeping three quarters of 80 gives 60 in a single step, with no subtraction at all.

problems.whyOnTest: Percentage questions are frequently answered with the discount rather than the price, and the choices here make that mistake reachable.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square of side 10 has a smaller square of side 4 cut out of one corner. What is the area of the shape that remains?

figure.alt: A large square of side 10 with a smaller square of side 4 removed from its top-right corner, leaving an L-shaped region shaded.

choices.misconception: I gave the area of the square that was cut out instead of the area that remains.
I subtracted the side length of the small square from the area of the big one.
I subtracted 4 rather than the small square's area of 16.
I gave the area of the whole square and forgot that a piece had been removed.

hints: Find the whole, find the hole, subtract.
Do not try to measure the L-shape directly. Work out the area of the big square and the area of the piece removed, then take one from the other.
The big square has area 10 x 10 = 100, the cut-out has area 4 x 4 = 16, so what remains is 100 - 16 = 84.

solutions.reliable: The big square has area 10 x 10 = 100. The removed square has area 4 x 4 = 16. The remaining shape has area 100 - 16 = 84. The transferable idea: for a shaded region that is what is left over, find the whole and the hole rather than measuring the odd shape directly.
solutions.elegant: Cut the L into a 10 by 6 rectangle and a 6 by 4 rectangle: 60 + 24 = 84, which is a useful check on the subtraction.

problems.whyOnTest: Shaded-region questions reward subtracting rather than measuring, and the wrong answers here come from subtracting the wrong quantity.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven cups all stand upside down. In one move you must turn over exactly two cups. Can all seven ever stand the right way up?

choices.misconception: I found a sequence that turned over most of the cups and assumed the last one could be fixed somehow.
I matched the number of moves to the number of cups without checking whether the target is reachable at all.

choices.text: Yes, but it takes many moves
choices.misconception: I assumed that with enough moves any arrangement can be reached.

choices.text: It depends which two cups you pick
choices.misconception: I thought the choice of which cups to flip could change whether the target is reachable.

hints: Count how many cups face up after each move.
Track the number of upward-facing cups. Every move changes that number by two or by nothing at all, so ask what that does to whether the number is odd or even.
Start with 0 cups up, which is even. Each move changes the count by +2, 0 or -2, so the count stays even forever. Seven is odd, so it can never be reached.

solutions.reliable: Count the cups facing up. At the start that is 0, which is even. A move turns over two cups, so it either adds 2, subtracts 2, or leaves the count unchanged - in every case the count stays even. Since 7 is odd, the target can never be reached, no matter how many moves you make. The transferable idea: find a quantity no move can change, and use it to rule the target out.
solutions.elegant: The parity of the number of upright cups is invariant, and it starts even while the goal is odd, so no sequence of moves connects them.

problems.whyOnTest: Proving something impossible is a different skill from finding an answer, and parity is the first tool students get for it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rope is 3.5 metres long. A second rope is 240 centimetres long. How much longer is the first rope, in centimetres?

choices.misconception: I subtracted correctly in metres but then gave the answer in metres when centimetres were asked for.
I converted 3.5 metres to 35 centimetres instead of 350.
I subtracted without converting at all, taking 3.5 away from 240.
I added the two lengths instead of finding the difference between them.

hints: Put both lengths in the same unit first.
Convert before you subtract, and check the direction of the conversion by asking whether the number should get bigger or smaller. Then check the units the answer is wanted in.
3.5 metres is 350 centimetres, and 350 - 240 = 110 centimetres.

solutions.reliable: Convert first: 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so 3.5 metres is 350 centimetres. Now subtract in matching units: 350 - 240 = 110 centimetres. The transferable idea: convert, then calculate, then check the answer is in the unit that was asked for.

problems.whyOnTest: Unit slips cost marks on questions students can otherwise do, and this one puts the slip in both the conversion and the final unit.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts 4, 7, 10, 13 and continues in the same way. What is the 20th term?

choices.misconception: I added the step 18 times, counting the gaps between terms one too few.
I multiplied the step of 3 by 20 and forgot that the first term is already in place.
I used a first term of 3 instead of 4 while adding 20 steps.
I added the step 20 times to the first term instead of 19 times.

hints: How many steps from the first term to the twentieth?
The terms go up by a fixed amount. To reach the 20th term from the 1st you take one fewer step than 20, because the first term costs no steps at all.
The step is 3. From term 1 to term 20 is 19 steps, so the 20th term is 4 + 19 x 3 = 4 + 57 = 61.

solutions.reliable: Each term is 3 more than the one before. Getting from the 1st term to the 20th takes 19 steps, not 20, because the first term is already there. So the 20th term is 4 + 19 x 3 = 4 + 57 = 61. Check on a small case: the 4th term should be 4 + 3 x 3 = 13, which matches. The transferable idea: count the gaps, not the terms.
solutions.elegant: The nth term is 3n + 1, so the 20th is 60 + 1 = 61.

problems.whyOnTest: The one-fewer-step rule is the single most common off-by-one in the patterns strand, and every distractor here is a version of getting it wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On the street grid shown you may only walk right or down. One junction is closed. How many routes go from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner?

figure.alt: A grid of streets with junctions arranged 4 across and 4 down. The junction one step right and one step down from the top-left corner is marked closed with a cross.

choices.misconception: I assumed closing one junction removes about half the routes and halved the total of 20.
I counted the routes that pass through the closed junction and gave that instead of the ones that avoid it.
I subtracted only the 2 routes that reach the closed junction, not all the routes that continue through it.
I counted every route on the open grid and forgot to remove the ones through the closed junction.

hints: Write a number into every junction.

The number of routes to a junction is the number of routes to the junction above it plus the number to the junction on its left. A closed junction simply gets a zero and everything downstream follows.
Fill the grid from the top-left. The top row and left column are all 1, the closed junction is 0, and adding down and across gives 8 at the bottom-right corner.

solutions.reliable: Label each junction with the number of routes that reach it. The top-left is 1, and every junction on the top row and the left column is 1 because there is a single way along the edge. Any other junction gets the sum of the junction above and the junction to its left, and the closed junction is set to 0. The rows come out as 1 1 1 1, then 1 0 1 2, then 1 1 2 4, then 1 2 4 8. So there are 8 routes. The transferable idea: build the count up junction by junction, and treat a blockage as a zero.
solutions.elegant: The open grid has 20 routes. The closed junction is reached by 2 routes and leads onward by 6, so 12 routes pass through it and 20 - 12 = 8 survive.

problems.whyOnTest: Grid paths are a classic 5-point figure, and filling the grid is the only method that keeps working once a junction is blocked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at exactly 3 o'clock?

figure.alt: A clock face with the hour hand pointing at 3 and the minute hand pointing at 12, with the angle between them marked.

choices.misconception: I gave the angle for one hour mark instead of the three hour marks between the hands.
I divided the right angle in half, as if a quarter of the clock were 45 degrees.
I used a third of the clock face rather than a quarter of it.
I read 3 o'clock as the hands pointing in opposite directions.

hints: Twelve hour marks fill 360 degrees.
Work out how many degrees one hour mark is worth, then count how many hour marks lie between the two hands at this exact time.
One hour mark is 360 divided by 12 = 30 degrees. At 3 o'clock the hands are 3 marks apart, so the angle is 3 x 30 = 90 degrees.

solutions.reliable: The 12 hour marks divide 360 degrees, so each mark is 30 degrees. At exactly 3 o'clock the minute hand is at 12 and the hour hand is at 3, which is 3 marks apart. The angle is 3 x 30 = 90 degrees. The transferable idea: convert hour marks to degrees once and reuse the 30 for every clock question.
solutions.elegant: Three o'clock is exactly a quarter turn round the face, and a quarter of 360 is 90.

problems.whyOnTest: It fixes the 30-degrees-per-hour-mark fact that every harder clock question is built on.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The mean of five numbers is 12. One of the numbers is removed and the mean of the remaining four is 11. What number was removed?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the two means from each other and gave the difference as the removed number.
I assumed the removed number must be the new mean, since the mean dropped to 11.
I assumed removing a number equal to the old mean is what changes the mean.
I added the two totals instead of subtracting one from the other.

hints: Turn each mean into a total.
A mean and a count give you a total. Find the total before the removal and the total after it; the difference between those totals is the number that left.
Five numbers with mean 12 total 60. Four numbers with mean 11 total 44. The removed number is 60 - 44 = 16.

solutions.reliable: Convert both means into totals. Five numbers averaging 12 have a total of 5 x 12 = 60. The remaining four averaging 11 have a total of 4 x 11 = 44. The number removed is 60 - 44 = 16. The transferable idea: a mean is only useful once you turn it into a total.
solutions.elegant: Removing the number dropped the mean of the other four by 1 each, so it carried 12 plus 4 extra, which is 16.

problems.whyOnTest: Contest questions almost always use the mean backwards, and going through totals is the only route that does not guess.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A 4 by 4 board has two opposite corner squares removed, leaving 14 squares. Each domino covers exactly two squares that share an edge. Can 7 dominoes cover the board?

figure.alt: A 4 by 4 chessboard-style grid coloured in alternating light and dark squares, with the top-left and bottom-right squares removed. Both removed squares were the same colour.

choices.text: Yes, and there is exactly one way
choices.misconception: I assumed that because 14 is even, seven dominoes must fit somehow.

choices.text: Yes, and there are several ways
choices.misconception: I tried a few arrangements, got most of the board covered, and assumed a full covering existed.

choices.text: No, because 14 is not divisible by 2
choices.misconception: I claimed the right answer for the wrong reason, since 14 is in fact divisible by 2.

choices.text: It depends which corners are removed
choices.misconception: I thought removing a different pair of opposite corners could change the colour balance, but opposite corners always share a colour.

choices.text: No, because the colours do not balance

hints: Colour the board like a chessboard.
A domino always covers one light and one dark square, whatever way it is placed. Count how many of each colour the board has after the corners are removed.
The full board has 8 light and 8 dark squares. Opposite corners are the same colour, so removing them leaves 8 of one colour and 6 of the other. Seven dominoes would need 7 of each.

solutions.reliable: Colour the board like a chessboard. Whichever way a domino is laid, it covers exactly one light and one dark square, so seven dominoes must cover 7 light and 7 dark squares. The full board has 8 of each, and the two removed corners are the same colour because opposite corners always are. That leaves 8 of one colour and 6 of the other, which no set of dominoes can cover. So it is impossible. The transferable idea: choose a colouring that forces every piece to cover a fixed mixture, then count.
solutions.elegant: Every domino is colour-balanced, so any coverable region must be too; removing two same-coloured squares destroys that balance immediately.

problems.whyOnTest: Colouring arguments prove impossibility in one line where trial and error can run forever, and this is the canonical example.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Eight people meet and everyone shakes hands with everyone else exactly once. How many handshakes take place?

choices.misconception: I doubled the number of people, as if each person made two handshakes in total.
I let each person shake hands with all eight people including themselves before halving.
I multiplied 8 by 7 and forgot that each handshake was counted from both sides.
I multiplied 8 by 8, counting every ordered pair including a person with themselves.

hints: Each handshake involves two people.
Count how many hands each person shakes, multiply by the number of people, and then correct for the fact that every handshake has been counted twice, once from each side.
Each of the 8 people shakes 7 hands, giving 8 x 7 = 56, but each handshake was counted twice, so the answer is 56 divided by 2 = 28.

solutions.reliable: Each of the 8 people shakes hands with the other 7, which gives 8 x 7 = 56 - but that counts every handshake twice, once from each participant. Halving gives 28. The transferable idea: when each object is counted once from each end, divide by two.
solutions.elegant: A handshake is a choice of 2 people from 8, and there are 8 x 7 divided by 2 = 28 such pairs.

problems.whyOnTest: The handshake shape reappears as lines between points and games in a league, and forgetting to halve is the universal error.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ravi cycles 12 km at 24 km per hour, then walks 6 km at 4 km per hour. How many minutes does the whole journey take?

choices.misconception: I worked out the cycling leg and gave that as the answer, forgetting the walk entirely.
I worked out the walking leg and gave that as the answer, forgetting the cycling entirely.
I wrote half an hour as 15 minutes instead of 30 and added it to the 90 minute walk.
I rounded the cycling leg up to a whole hour instead of keeping it as half an hour.

hints: Work out each leg on its own.
Time is distance divided by speed, so do the two legs separately and add the times. Convert both to minutes before adding so nothing is left in mixed units.
Cycling: 12 divided by 24 is half an hour, which is 30 minutes. Walking: 6 divided by 4 is one and a half hours, which is 90 minutes. Together that is 120 minutes.

solutions.reliable: Do each leg separately. Cycling 12 km at 24 km/h takes 12 divided by 24 = 0.5 hours, or 30 minutes. Walking 6 km at 4 km/h takes 6 divided by 4 = 1.5 hours, or 90 minutes. The whole journey is 30 + 90 = 120 minutes. The transferable idea: add times, never average speeds, and convert to one unit before adding.

problems.whyOnTest: Journeys in two legs test whether a student computes each leg separately and keeps the units consistent while adding.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the units digit of 7 multiplied by itself 2026 times, that is 7 to the power 2026?

choices.text: it cannot be found without a calculator
choices.misconception: I assumed a number this large has no reachable last digit and gave up on the cycle.
I found the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 but used a remainder of 0 when the remainder is actually 2.
I found the cycle but counted its positions starting at zero, shifting my answer along by one.
I assumed the units digit of any power of 7 is always 7.

hints: List the last digits of the first few powers.
The last digit of a product depends only on the last digits multiplied. Work out the last digits of the first few powers until they repeat, then use the remainder to find the position.
The last digits go 7, 9, 3, 1 and then repeat every 4. 2026 divided by 4 is 506 remainder 2, so the answer is the second in the cycle, which is 9.

solutions.reliable: The last digit of a product depends only on the last digits of the factors, so build the cycle: 7 to the power 1 ends in 7, then 49 ends in 9, then 343 ends in 3, then 2401 ends in 1, then it starts again at 7. The cycle has length 4. Divide 2026 by 4 to get 506 remainder 2, so the answer sits at position 2 of the cycle, which is 9. The transferable idea: find the cycle, then use the remainder as a position within it.
solutions.elegant: Powers of 7 repeat their last digit every 4 steps, and 2026 is 2 more than a multiple of 4, so it ends like 7 squared - in 9.

problems.whyOnTest: It looks impossible without a calculator and takes twenty seconds with the cycle, which is exactly the kind of trade a 5-point question rewards.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A solid block is built from unit cubes and measures 4 by 3 by 2. How many unit cubes does it contain?

figure.alt: A rectangular block built from unit cubes, 4 cubes long, 3 cubes deep and 2 cubes tall, drawn so that both layers are visible.

choices.misconception: I added the three measurements together instead of multiplying them.
I counted one layer of 4 by 3 and forgot that the block is two layers tall.
I read the block as 3 by 3 by 2 because the drawing hid the far column.
I counted only the cubes whose faces I could actually see in the picture.

hints: Count one layer, then count the layers.
A solid block is layers of the same size stacked up. Work out how many cubes are in one horizontal layer, then multiply by the number of layers.
One layer is 4 x 3 = 12 cubes and there are 2 layers, so 12 x 2 = 24.

solutions.reliable: One horizontal layer is 4 by 3, which is 12 cubes. The block is 2 layers tall, so it holds 12 x 2 = 24 unit cubes. The transferable idea: counting a layer at a time reaches the cubes you cannot see, and it keeps working when the layers are not all the same size.

problems.whyOnTest: It anchors the layer-by-layer habit before the harder hidden-cube questions where the layers differ in size.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A flag shape is rotated a quarter turn clockwise about its bottom-left corner. Which of the descriptions matches the result?

figure.alt: A flag shape drawn as an upright pole with a small triangle attached to the top right of the pole, standing on a marked corner point at the bottom of the pole.

choices.text: the pole points right and the triangle is below it
the pole points right and the triangle is above it
choices.misconception: I turned the pole the right way but kept the triangle on the side it started on.

choices.text: the pole points left and the triangle is above it
choices.misconception: I turned the shape anticlockwise instead of clockwise.

choices.text: the pole points down and the triangle is to the left
choices.misconception: I turned the shape half a turn instead of a quarter turn.

choices.text: the pole points up and the triangle is on the left
choices.misconception: I reflected the shape in a vertical line instead of rotating it.

hints: Turn the page, do not imagine it.
A quarter turn clockwise sends up to the right. Track the pole first, then ask which side of the pole the triangle ends up on - it travels with the pole, it does not stay put.
Up becomes right, so the pole points right. The triangle was on the right of an upward pole, and turning clockwise carries it to below a rightward pole.

solutions.reliable: Track one part at a time. A quarter turn clockwise sends the direction up to the direction right, so the upright pole ends up pointing right. The triangle sat on the right-hand side of the upward pole; clockwise, right becomes down, so the triangle ends up below the rightward pole. The transferable idea: rotate each feature by the same rule rather than picturing the whole shape at once.

problems.whyOnTest: Rotation questions are answered wrongly when a student turns the main feature but leaves the details where they were.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A drawer holds 10 red socks, 10 blue socks and 10 green socks, all mixed up in the dark. How many socks must you take out to be sure of having a matching pair?

choices.misconception: I answered with the lucky case, where the first two socks happen to match.
I used the number of colours as my answer without adding one for the sock that must repeat.
I worked from the number of socks of each colour instead of the number of colours.
I took the whole drawer, guaranteeing a pair but far more socks than are needed.

hints: Imagine the unluckiest possible draw.
Ask how many socks you could take while still having no pair at all. One more than that number forces a match, because there is nowhere new for it to go.
The worst case is one sock of each colour, which is 3 socks and still no pair. The fourth sock must repeat a colour, so 4 socks are enough.

solutions.reliable: Think about the worst case rather than the lucky one. You could draw one red, one blue and one green - three socks with no matching pair. But a fourth sock must be red, blue or green, so it repeats a colour you already hold. Four socks therefore guarantee a pair, and three do not. The transferable idea: fill every box once, then add one.
solutions.elegant: With 3 colours acting as boxes, 4 socks cannot all go in different boxes, so two share a box - that is the pigeonhole principle in one line.

problems.whyOnTest: To be sure means the worst case, and answering with the lucky case is the single most common misreading in the counting strand.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: One bus leaves every 12 minutes and another every 18 minutes. They leave together at 9:00. When do they next leave together?

choices.misconception: I found the greatest common divisor of 12 and 18 instead of the least common multiple.
I added the two intervals together rather than looking for a time that is a multiple of both.
I found a common multiple but not the least one, landing on a later coincidence.
I multiplied the two intervals together instead of finding their least common multiple.

hints: List the departure times for each bus.
You want the first time that is a multiple of both intervals. Listing the multiples of each and finding the first one they share is quicker than any formula at these sizes.
Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. Multiples of 18: 18, 36. The first shared one is 36 minutes, so 9:36.

solutions.reliable: List the minutes after 9:00 at which each bus leaves. The first bus goes at 12, 24, 36, 48; the second at 18, 36, 54. The first time both appear is 36 minutes, so they next leave together at 9:36. The transferable idea: two repeating cycles coincide at their least common multiple.
solutions.elegant: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, so the least common multiple is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36.

problems.whyOnTest: Coinciding cycles is the standard dressing for least common multiple, and reaching for the greatest common divisor instead is the reliable error.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A photograph is enlarged so that each side becomes 3 times as long. How many times bigger is its area?

choices.misconception: I applied the length scale factor straight to the area.
I doubled the scale factor because area involves two dimensions, instead of squaring it.
I multiplied the scale factor by four, as though area scaled with the number of sides.
I cubed the scale factor, which is the rule for volume rather than area.

hints: Try it on a small rectangle first.
Take a rectangle you can compute, triple both sides, and compare the two areas. The relationship you find holds for any shape, not just that rectangle.
A 2 by 5 rectangle has area 10. Tripled it becomes 6 by 15 with area 90, which is 9 times as much. Area scales by the square of the length factor.

solutions.reliable: Test it concretely. A 2 by 5 rectangle has area 10. After tripling each side it is 6 by 15, with area 90 - nine times the original. In general, tripling both dimensions multiplies the area by 3 x 3 = 9. The transferable idea: length scales by k, area by k squared, volume by k cubed.
solutions.elegant: Nine copies of the original photo tile the enlarged one exactly, three across and three down.

problems.whyOnTest: Applying a length scale factor to an area is one of the highest-frequency errors across the whole exam, at every band.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag holds 5 black and 6 white stones. You repeatedly remove two stones: if they match you put a black one in, if they differ you put a white one in. What colour is the last stone?

choices.misconception: I noticed there are more white stones than black ones and guessed the majority colour would survive.

choices.text: it depends on the order of the moves
choices.misconception: I tried a few orders, saw different-looking positions along the way, and assumed the ending must vary too.

choices.text: the bag never gets down to one stone
choices.misconception: I did not notice that every move takes two stones out and puts one back, so the count falls by exactly one each time.

choices.text: white if the first two stones match
choices.misconception: I assumed the first move settles the outcome instead of looking for a quantity that no move can change.

hints: Watch what happens to the number of white stones.
Check each kind of move and ask how the white count changes. If it only ever changes by an even amount, then whether it is odd or even can never change at all.

Two blacks: white count unchanged. Two whites: white count falls by 2. One of each: one white out, one white in, so unchanged. The white count starts at 6 and stays even, so the last stone cannot be white.

solutions.reliable: Track the number of white stones. Two blacks out and a black in leaves it unchanged. Two whites out and a black in lowers it by 2. One of each out and a white in removes one white and returns one, leaving it unchanged. Every move therefore changes the white count by 0 or by 2, so it stays even forever. It starts at 6, which is even, so the final single stone cannot be white - it is black. The transferable idea: find a quantity no move can change, and the ending is decided before you start.
solutions.elegant: The parity of the white count is invariant, so the answer depends only on whether the bag starts with an odd or even number of white stones - never on how you play.

problems.whyOnTest: Invariants turn an unbounded search into one observation, and this is the cleanest place for a student to meet the idea.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: One tap fills a tank in 6 hours and another fills it in 3 hours. With both running, how long does the tank take to fill?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the two times from each other rather than adding the rates.
I averaged the two times, which would only be right if the taps took turns instead of running together.
I added the two times together, which makes the tank slower with two taps than with one.
I used the faster tap's time alone and ignored the contribution of the slower one.

hints: Ask how much each tap fills in one hour.
Work in tanks per hour rather than hours per tank. Add the two hourly amounts to get how much the pair fills in an hour, then turn that back into a time.
In one hour the first tap fills one sixth and the second fills one third, which is two sixths. Together that is three sixths, or half the tank, so the whole tank takes 2 hours.

solutions.reliable: Switch to rates. In one hour the first tap fills 1/6 of the tank and the second fills 1/3 = 2/6. Together they fill 3/6 = 1/2 of the tank per hour, so the full tank takes 2 hours. Sanity check: two taps must be faster than the faster tap alone, and 2 hours is less than 3. The transferable idea: add rates, never times.
solutions.elegant: The second tap is twice as fast as the first, so together they work at three times the first tap's rate and take a third of its 6 hours.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding times instead of rates produces an answer slower than one tap alone, and spotting that absurdity is itself the lesson.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A number is 4 more than a third of itself. Which of the choices is that number?

choices.misconception: I tested the smallest choice first and stopped at the first one that felt about right.
I read a third of itself as three times itself and solved the wrong equation.
I reversed the comparison, finding a number whose third is 4 less than itself in the wrong direction.
I picked the largest choice because dividing by three made me expect a big starting number.

hints: Test a choice instead of solving.
The answer is one of the five. Take a middle choice, find a third of it, add 4, and see whether you land back on the number you started with.
Test 12: a third is 4, and 4 + 4 = 8, not 12, so 12 is too big. Test 6: a third is 2, and 2 + 4 = 6. That works.

solutions.reliable: Back-solve. Take a choice, find a third of it, add 4, and check whether you land back on the same number. For 12: a third is 4, and 4 + 4 = 8, which is not 12, so 12 is too big. For 6: a third is 2, and 2 + 4 = 6 - it works. Starting from a middle choice tells you which direction to move next. The transferable idea: on a multiple-choice paper, checking an answer is often far cheaper than deriving it.
solutions.elegant: Writing n = n/3 + 4 gives 2n/3 = 4, so n = 6 - worth doing as a check even when you back-solved.

problems.whyOnTest: Back-solving is a contest skill in its own right, and knowing when checking beats deriving is worth several marks across a paper.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a 4 by 4 board, how many aligned squares of any size are there, counting 1 by 1, 2 by 2, 3 by 3 and 4 by 4?

choices.misconception: I counted only the sixteen smallest squares and stopped there.
I counted the small squares and the single big one, and forgot every size in between.
I counted the 2 by 2 squares as four rather than nine, splitting the board into blocks.
I used 4 by 4 positions for every size instead of shrinking the range as the square grows.

hints: Do each size separately, largest first.
For a square of side k on a 4 by 4 board, the top-left corner can sit in 5 minus k columns and 5 minus k rows. Work out that count for each size and add.

solutions.reliable: Take the sizes one at a time. A square of side k has its top-left corner in (5 - k) columns and (5 - k) rows. Side 1 gives 16, side 2 gives 9, side 3 gives 4, side 4 gives 1. Adding: 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30. The transferable idea: count by size, and let the sliding range shrink as the shape grows.
solutions.elegant: The total is the sum of the first four square numbers, which is 30 - the same shape of answer on any n by n board.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting by size is the habit that stops a student missing the middle sizes, and this is the cleanest place to practise it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 9 are placed in a row in some order. Can every neighbouring pair add up to an odd number?

choices.text: Yes, but only one order works
choices.misconception: I found one arrangement that works and assumed a problem this fiddly could only have one answer.

choices.text: No, there are too many odd numbers
choices.misconception: I saw five odd numbers against four even ones and called that a mismatch, when a row of nine needs exactly five of one and four of the other.

choices.text: No, nine places is an odd number of places
choices.misconception: I blamed the length of the row rather than checking how many odd and even numbers it has to hold.

choices.text: Only if the row starts with an even number
choices.misconception: I decided the first number settles it without checking that starting even would need five even numbers, and only four exist.

hints: Odd plus even is odd. What does that force?
A pair adds to an odd number only when one is odd and one is even, so the whole row has to alternate. Then count how many odd and even numbers you actually have.
Alternating nine places needs five of one parity and four of the other. The numbers 1 to 9 give exactly five odd and four even, so an alternating row exists - and it must start and end odd.

solutions.reliable: A pair adds to an odd number exactly when one member is odd and the other even, so the row must alternate parity all the way along. Nine alternating places need five of one parity and four of the other, and 1 to 9 gives exactly five odd numbers and four even ones. So it can be done, with the odd numbers in the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth places - for example 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Many orders work: the five odd numbers can be arranged among their places in any order, and so can the four even ones. The transferable idea: turn a question about sums into a question about parity, then count the parities you have.
solutions.elegant: Alternation is forced, the parity counts match exactly, so the natural order 1 to 9 already works and every reshuffle within each parity works too.

problems.whyOnTest: It looks like a search and is really a counting-by-parity argument, which is the jump a 5-point question asks a student to make.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A circle of radius 5 is drawn inside a square of side 10, touching all four sides. What fraction of the square is outside the circle, to the nearest tenth?

figure.alt: A square with a circle drawn inside it, the circle touching the midpoint of each of the four sides. The region inside the square but outside the circle is shaded.

choices.misconception: I estimated by eye from the four corner pieces without comparing them to the whole square.
I used a diameter of 5 instead of a radius of 5 when working out the circle's area.
I assumed the circle covers half the square because it touches all four sides.
I found the fraction covered by the circle and gave that instead of the fraction outside it.

hints: Find the whole and the hole, then subtract.
Work out the area of the square and the area of the circle separately, subtract to get the shaded region, and only then turn it into a fraction of the square.
The square is 10 x 10 = 100. The circle is pi times 5 squared, about 78.5. The region outside is about 21.5, which is about 0.2 of the square.

solutions.reliable: The square has area 10 x 10 = 100. The circle has radius 5, so its area is pi times 25, about 78.5. The shaded region is 100 - 78.5 = 21.5, which as a fraction of the square is 0.215, or 0.2 to the nearest tenth. The transferable idea: subtract to get the odd-shaped region, then convert to a fraction last.
solutions.elegant: The circle takes up pi over 4 of any square it is inscribed in, about 0.785, so the corners always keep about 0.215 - the side length never matters.

problems.whyOnTest: Inscribed-circle questions recur at every band, and the pi-over-four fact turns them into one step regardless of the numbers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when 2 to the power 30 is divided by 7?

choices.misconception: I found the cycle 2, 4, 1 but read the remainder of 30 divided by 3 as one instead of zero.
I counted the cycle positions from zero, which shifted my answer one step along.
I divided 30 by 7 and used that remainder rather than the remainder of the powers.
I assumed the remainder would be one less than the divisor because the power is large.

hints: Work out the first few powers and their remainders.
Remainders of powers repeat on a short cycle. Find the remainders of 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on when divided by 7, and stop as soon as the list starts repeating.
The remainders go 2, 4, 1, then 2, 4, 1 again - a cycle of length 3. Since 30 is a multiple of 3, the answer is the last of the cycle, which is 1.

solutions.reliable: Build the cycle of remainders. 2 leaves 2, 4 leaves 4, 8 leaves 1, 16 leaves 2, 32 leaves 4, 64 leaves 1 - so the remainders repeat every 3 powers as 2, 4, 1. Because 30 divides exactly by 3, the thirtieth power sits at the end of a full cycle, giving remainder 1. The transferable idea: a remainder of zero lands on the last entry of the cycle, not the first.
solutions.elegant: 2 cubed is 8, which is one more than 7, so 2 to the power 30 is (2 cubed) to the power 10, which leaves the same remainder as 1 to the power 10 - namely 1.

problems.whyOnTest: It is the remainder cycle again with a bigger modulus, and the remainder-of-zero edge case is exactly where students slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

choices.misconception: I found the sum of 1 to 50 and forgot that every term here is twice as big.
I used 49 pairs instead of 25, losing one pair from the count.
I estimated the answer as a round number rather than pairing properly.
I paired the terms but forgot that pairing counts every number twice, so I never halved.

hints: Pair the outside in, then count the pairs.
Every term is even, so the whole sum is twice the sum of 1 to 50. Alternatively pair 2 with 100, 4 with 98, and so on, and count how many pairs fifty terms give.
There are 50 terms, so 25 pairs, each adding to 102. That is 25 x 102 = 2550.

solutions.reliable: There are 50 even numbers from 2 to 100. Pair the outside in: 2 + 100 = 102, 4 + 98 = 102, and so on, giving 25 pairs of 102. The total is 25 x 102 = 2550. Check the other way: the sum is twice 1 + 2 + ... + 50 = 2 x 1275 = 2550. The transferable idea: two routes that agree is worth more than one route checked twice.
solutions.elegant: Every term is double the matching term of 1 to 50, so the sum is twice 1275, which is 2550.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting the pairs is where this goes wrong: fifty terms make twenty-five pairs, not fifty and not forty-nine.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A tap drips about 3 times a minute. Roughly how many drips is that in one day?

choices.misconception: I worked out the drips in an hour and stopped there.
I multiplied by the 24 hours but forgot the 60 minutes in each one.
I used 6 hours in a day, thinking of waking hours rather than a whole day.
I used 600 minutes in an hour rather than 60.

hints: Go minute, then hour, then day.
Build the answer one unit at a time rather than in one leap: drips per minute, then per hour, then per day. Check after each step whether the number should have grown.
3 a minute is 3 x 60 = 180 an hour, and 180 x 24 = 4320 a day.

solutions.reliable: Take it one unit at a time. Three drips a minute is 3 x 60 = 180 an hour. Over 24 hours that is 180 x 24 = 4320. The transferable idea: convert one step at a time and sanity-check the size after each step, rather than multiplying everything at once and hoping.
solutions.elegant: A day is about 1440 minutes, and three times that is a little over 4000 - enough to pick the right choice without finishing the arithmetic.

problems.whyOnTest: Order-of-magnitude questions are answered by picking the nearest choice, and a single missed conversion moves the answer by a factor of sixty.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A and B are different digits. The two-digit number AB added to the two-digit number BA gives 132. What is A + B?

choices.misconception: I added the digits of 132 instead of working out what A and B must be.
I found A + B correctly and then halved it, as if the question wanted one digit.
I spotted the 11 in the working and gave that instead of the sum it multiplies.
I found a pair of digits by trial and misadded them by one.

hints: Write both numbers out in tens and ones.
AB means ten A plus B, and BA means ten B plus A. Add those two expressions and see what the total is a multiple of. The answer falls out without finding A and B separately.

solutions.reliable: Write each number in terms of its digits. AB is 10A + B and BA is 10B + A. Adding gives 11A + 11B, which is 11 times (A + B). So 11(A + B) = 132, and A + B = 132 divided by 11 = 12. You never need to know A and B separately - and in fact several pairs work, such as 48 and 84. The transferable idea: write the digits out algebraically and the structure appears.
solutions.elegant: Any two-digit number plus its reverse is 11 times the digit sum, so the answer is 132 divided by 11.

problems.whyOnTest: It rewards writing a digit puzzle out in tens and ones instead of guessing pairs, which is the technique every harder cryptarithm needs.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: 24 pencils and 36 erasers are shared into identical gift bags, using every item. What is the largest number of bags possible?

choices.misconception: I found a number that divides both but not the largest one, stopping at the first that worked.
I used the difference between 36 and 24 divided by 2 rather than a common factor.
I used a factor of 36 without checking that it also divides 24.
I found the least common multiple instead of the greatest common divisor.

hints: The bags must be identical, so the number divides both.
Every bag holds the same number of pencils and the same number of erasers, so the number of bags divides 24 and divides 36. You want the largest number that does both.
The common factors of 24 and 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. The largest is 12, giving 2 pencils and 3 erasers per bag.

solutions.reliable: Identical bags with nothing left over means the number of bags divides both 24 and 36. List the factors: 24 gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 and 36 gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. The largest number in both lists is 12, so 12 bags, each with 2 pencils and 3 erasers. The transferable idea: sharing equally with nothing left over is a greatest-common-divisor question, while coinciding cycles are a least-common-multiple one.
solutions.elegant: 24 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 and 36 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3, so the shared part is 2 x 2 x 3 = 12.

problems.whyOnTest: Choosing between the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple is the whole question, and picking the wrong one gives an answer that looks reasonable.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three quarters of a class of 28 travelled by bus. How many did not travel by bus?

choices.misconception: I divided 28 by 7 instead of taking a quarter of it.
I found three quarters of 16 by mistake, mixing up the class size.
I found how many did travel by bus and gave that instead of how many did not.
I subtracted the 4 quarters as if they were 4 students.

hints: What fraction did not travel by bus?
If three quarters went by bus, the rest is one quarter. Taking one quarter of the class directly is one step; working out three quarters and subtracting is two.
One quarter of 28 is 7, so 7 students did not travel by bus.

solutions.reliable: Three quarters went by bus, so one quarter did not. One quarter of 28 is 28 divided by 4 = 7. Check the other way: three quarters is 21, and 28 - 21 = 7. The transferable idea: when a question asks about the rest, find the fraction that is left over first - it is fewer steps and fewer chances to slip.

problems.whyOnTest: Answering with the quantity you computed rather than the one that was asked for is the single most common lost mark on the whole paper.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A price goes up by 20%, then down by 20%. Compared with the original price, the final price is:

choices.misconception: I applied only the decrease and forgot that the price had already risen.
I assumed a rise and a fall of the same percentage cancel each other out exactly.
I got the size of the change right but the direction wrong.
I added the two percentages together instead of applying them one after the other.

hints: Start from 100 and follow it through.
Pick a convenient starting price and apply the two changes in order. The second percentage is taken of the new price, not the original one, which is the whole point.
Start at 100. Up 20% gives 120. Down 20% of 120 is a fall of 24, giving 96 - which is 4% below 100.

solutions.reliable: Take a starting price of 100. A 20% rise gives 120. A 20% fall is now 20% of 120, which is 24, so the price becomes 96. That is 4 below 100, or 4% lower. The transferable idea: name what the percentage is a percentage of, every single time - the second one is not of the original price.
solutions.elegant: Multiplying by 1.2 and then by 0.8 gives 0.96 whatever the starting price, so the order does not matter and the loss is always 4%.

problems.whyOnTest: The belief that a rise and a fall of the same percentage cancel is one of the most durable misconceptions in the whole syllabus.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The mean of four numbers is 9. Three of them are 5, 8 and 12. What is the fourth?

choices.misconception: I assumed the missing number must be the mean itself.
I averaged the three known numbers instead of working from the total.
I repeated one of the numbers already given rather than computing the missing one.
I used a total of 37 instead of 36, adding the mean in once too often.

hints: Turn the mean into a total first.
Four numbers with a mean of 9 have a fixed total. Work that total out, add up the three you know, and the difference is the one you do not.
The total is 4 x 9 = 36. The three known numbers add to 5 + 8 + 12 = 25, so the fourth is 36 - 25 = 11.

solutions.reliable: A mean of 9 across four numbers means the total is 4 x 9 = 36. The three given numbers add to 25, so the missing one is 36 - 25 = 11. Check: 5 + 8 + 12 + 11 = 36, and 36 divided by 4 is 9. The transferable idea: a mean is only useful once you have turned it into a total.
solutions.elegant: Measure each number against the mean: 5 is 4 below, 8 is 1 below, 12 is 3 above, a net 2 below. The last number must be 2 above the mean, so 11.

problems.whyOnTest: Almost every contest mean question runs backwards from the mean, and going through the total is the only route that does not guess.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a class of 30, 18 play football and 14 play chess. 6 play both. How many play neither?

choices.misconception: I added 18 and 14 without removing the overlap, then subtracted from 30.
I subtracted the 6 who play both twice instead of once.
I subtracted only the footballers from the class and forgot the chess players entirely.
I found how many play at least one sport and gave that instead of how many play neither.

hints: Fill in the middle of the two circles first.
Draw two overlapping circles and write the 6 who do both in the overlap. The rest of each circle is what is left after taking the overlap out, and everything outside is the answer.
Playing at least one is 18 + 14 - 6 = 26. So 30 - 26 = 4 play neither.

solutions.reliable: Adding 18 and 14 counts the 6 who do both twice, so the number playing at least one is 18 + 14 - 6 = 26. Everyone else plays neither: 30 - 26 = 4. Drawing it confirms the parts: 12 football only, 6 both, 8 chess only, 4 neither - and 12 + 6 + 8 + 4 = 30. The transferable idea: fill the overlap in first, then the rest follows.

problems.whyOnTest: Two overlapping groups is one of the most reliably examined shapes at this level, and the double-counted overlap is the whole difficulty.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five children sit in a row. Two of them are twins who insist on sitting next to each other. In how many orders can the five sit?

choices.misconception: I treated the twins as one child and forgot they can also swap places with each other.
I glued the twins together into a single block but then forgot that the block can be arranged with the others in more ways than I counted.
I halved the 120 total, assuming the twins are together in exactly half the arrangements.
I counted every arrangement of five children and forgot the twins' condition entirely.

hints: Glue the twins together into one block.
Treat the pair as a single object, so you are arranging four things rather than five. Then remember the two inside the block can be in either order.
Four objects arrange in 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 ways, and the twins can be either way round inside the block, so 24 x 2 = 48.

solutions.reliable: Tie the twins together and treat them as one object. You now have four objects to arrange, which can be done in 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 ways. Inside the block the twins can sit in 2 orders, so the total is 24 x 2 = 48. Sanity check: 48 is less than the 120 unrestricted arrangements, as it must be. The transferable idea: place the restricted objects first by gluing them, then multiply by their internal orders.
solutions.elegant: The twins occupy one of 4 adjacent pairs of seats, in 2 orders, and the other three children fill the rest in 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways: 4 x 2 x 6 = 48.

problems.whyOnTest: The glue-them-together move is the standard technique for a must-sit-together restriction, and forgetting the internal swap halves the answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Five beads of five different colours are threaded on a circular bracelet. Two bracelets count as the same if one can be turned or flipped into the other. How many different bracelets are there?

choices.misconception: I divided the 120 arrangements by 6 rather than by the 10 movements that leave a bracelet looking the same.
I allowed for turning the bracelet but forgot it can also be flipped over.
I halved the 120 for flipping but forgot that turning also gives the same bracelet.
I counted every arrangement in a line, as if the bracelet had a fixed first bead.

hints: Count the arrangements, then count the repeats.

Start from all the arrangements as if the positions were fixed. Then work out how many of those are really the same bracelet: each one appears once per turn and again for each turn of the flipped version.
There are 120 arrangements. Each bracelet appears 5 times from turning and twice over from flipping, so 10 times in all: 120 divided by 10 = 12.

solutions.reliable: Overcount deliberately, then correct. Five distinct beads in five fixed positions give 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120 arrangements. But turning the bracelet by one, two, three or four positions gives the same bracelet, and so does flipping it over and turning it. That is 5 turns times 2 for the flip = 10 arrangements per genuine bracelet. So 120 divided by 10 = 12. The transferable idea: name exactly how many times each object was counted before dividing.
solutions.elegant: Hold one bead fixed to kill the turning, leaving 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 arrangements of the rest, then halve for the flip: 12.

problems.whyOnTest: Deliberate overcounting followed by an exact correction is a genuine 5-point idea, and guessing the correction factor is what separates a right answer from a plausible one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi
