problems.whyOnTest: Elimination grids are won by starting from the most constrained row, and the choices reward guessing before that.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bread recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 5 to 3. The two together weigh 320 grams. How much of that is flour?

choices.misconception: I worked out the part size correctly and then answered for the sugar instead of the flour.
I split the 320 grams into two halves instead of into eight equal parts.
I took three fifths of 320 rather than five eighths, using the ratio numbers as a fraction of each other.
I divided 320 by the 5 in the ratio and stopped, treating 5 as the number of parts.

hints: The ratio counts parts, not grams.
Five parts flour and three parts sugar make eight parts altogether. Find what one part weighs first.
320 divided by 8 is 40 grams per part. Flour is five parts, so 5 times 40 = 200 grams.

solutions.reliable: A ratio of 5 to 3 means the mixture is made of 5 + 3 = 8 equal parts. Divide the total by the number of parts: 320 / 8 = 40 grams per part. Flour is 5 parts, so it weighs 5 x 40 = 200 grams (and sugar is 3 x 40 = 120 grams, which checks out because 200 + 120 = 320). The transferable move: turn a ratio into a part size before you touch either quantity. The transferable idea: turn a ratio into a part size before you touch either quantity.
solutions.elegant: Flour is 5 of the 8 parts, so it is five eighths of 320, and five eighths of 320 is 200.

problems.whyOnTest: Almost every ratio mistake is answering for the wrong part or forgetting the parts must add to the whole.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a triangle, one angle measures 30 degrees. Of the other two angles, one is exactly twice the other. What is the largest angle in the triangle?

choices.misconception: I found the smaller of the two unknown angles and stopped before doubling it.
I split the remaining 150 degrees into two equal halves instead of a one-to-two split.
I split the remainder evenly into 75 and 75, then doubled one of them.
I assumed that the largest angle in a triangle like this must be a right angle.

hints: The three angles add to 180 degrees, so the two unknown ones add to 150.
Call the smaller unknown angle x. Then the other is 2x, and x + 2x = 150.
3x = 150, so x = 50 and 2x = 100. The angles are 30, 50 and 100, which sum to 180.

solutions.reliable: The angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees, so the two unknown angles together make 180 - 30 = 150. Writing the smaller as x makes the larger 2x, so x + 2x = 3x = 150 and x = 50. The two unknown angles are therefore 50 and 100, and the largest angle in the triangle is 100 degrees. Check: 30 + 50 + 100 = 180. The transferable idea: naming the smaller share x keeps an uneven split from collapsing into an even one.
solutions.elegant: The remainder of 150 splits into three equal shares of 50; the larger angle takes two of them, giving 100.

problems.whyOnTest: Naming the smaller quantity x is what keeps a one-to-two split from collapsing into an even one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A jacket costs 80 pounds. In January the price rises by 20 percent. In February the new price falls by 20 percent. What is the price at the end of February?

choices.misconception: I assumed a 20 percent rise and a 20 percent fall must cancel because the percentages match.
I applied only the fall and forgot the rise.
I got the size of the change right but the direction wrong.
I applied only the rise and forgot the fall.

hints: The two 20 percents are not taken from the same amount.
The rise is 20 percent of 80. The fall is 20 percent of the NEW price, which is bigger.
80 x 1.2 = 96, then 96 x 0.8 = 76.80. The jacket ends up cheaper than it started.

solutions.reliable: Work the two changes in order and never reuse the old base. The rise: 80 x 1.2 = 96 pounds. The fall is 20 percent of 96, not of 80, so the new price is 96 x 0.8 = 76.80 pounds. The jacket ends 3.20 pounds cheaper than it began. The transferable idea: a percentage is always a percentage OF something, and after the first change that something has moved.
solutions.elegant: Multiplying by 1.2 and then by 0.8 is multiplying by 0.96, so any starting price ends 4 percent lower.

problems.whyOnTest: The belief that equal percentage rises and falls cancel is one of the most common errors on the paper.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a class of 30 students, 18 play football and 15 play chess. Exactly 7 students do both. How many students play neither?

choices.misconception: I found how many students play at least one of the two and answered with that instead.
I added 18 and 15 to get 33, subtracted the 30 in the class, and used the 3 left over.
I removed the 7 from both groups and subtracted 11 and 8 from 30, taking the overlap away twice.
I answered with the number who play both, which is what the question gave me rather than what it asked for.

hints: Adding 18 and 15 counts the 7 who do both twice.
Work out how many play at least one sport first, then take that away from the class.
18 + 15 - 7 = 26 play at least one. 30 - 26 = 4 play neither.

solutions.reliable: Adding the two groups counts every student who does both exactly twice, so subtract the overlap once to correct it: 18 + 15 - 7 = 26 students play at least one of the two. Everyone else plays neither, so the answer is 30 - 26 = 4. A useful check is to split the class into four boxes: 11 football only, 8 chess only, 7 both, 4 neither, and 11 + 8 + 7 + 4 = 30. The transferable idea: when two groups overlap, add them and subtract the overlap exactly once.
solutions.elegant: Football only is 11 and chess only is 8, so 11 + 8 + 7 = 26 are accounted for and 4 are left.

problems.whyOnTest: Two overlapping groups appear on every paper, and the whole difficulty is remembering to subtract the overlap exactly once.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A photograph measures 8 cm by 12 cm. It is enlarged so that the shorter side becomes 20 cm, and the shape is not distorted. How long is the longer side of the enlargement?

choices.misconception: I kept the difference of 4 cm between the two sides instead of keeping their ratio.
I added 20 to 12 rather than scaling 12.
I used the scale factor upside down and multiplied 12 by 8/20 instead of 20/8.
I multiplied 12 by 1.5, the ratio between the original sides, instead of by the enlargement factor.

hints: An enlargement multiplies both sides by the same number.
The shorter side went from 8 to 20. What number multiplies 8 to give 20?
20 / 8 = 2.5, so the longer side is 12 x 2.5 = 30 cm.

solutions.reliable: An enlargement multiplies every length by one scale factor. The shorter side went from 8 cm to 20 cm, so the factor is 20 / 8 = 2.5. Applying the same factor to the longer side gives 12 x 2.5 = 30 cm. Check the shape is preserved by comparing ratios: 8/12 = 20/30 = 2/3. The transferable idea: enlargements multiply, they do not add.
solutions.elegant: The sides are in the ratio 2 to 3, so a shorter side of 20 forces a longer side of 30.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding a constant instead of multiplying is the single most common scaling error, and it always distorts the shape.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A pattern is built in rows. The first figure has 1 row, the second has 2 rows, and so on. In every figure, the first row has 1 dot, the second has 3 dots, the third has 5 dots, and each row after has 2 more dots than the one above it. How many dots are in the eighth figure?

choices.misconception: I gave the number of dots in the eighth ROW instead of the whole figure.
I added the row numbers 1 through 8 instead of the odd numbers of dots.
I multiplied 8 rows by 9, using a rough average row that is one too large.
I counted the rows starting from zero and used the ninth square number.

hints: Write out the rows for a small figure and add them, before trying figure eight.
Figure 1 has 1 dot. Figure 2 has 1 + 3 = 4. Figure 3 has 1 + 3 + 5 = 9. Those are square numbers.
The nth figure holds n squared dots, so the eighth holds 8 x 8 = 64.

solutions.reliable: Build the small cases first. Figure 1 is 1 dot; figure 2 is 1 + 3 = 4; figure 3 is 1 + 3 + 5 = 9; figure 4 is 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. Those are 1, 4, 9, 16 - the square numbers - so the nth figure holds n squared dots and the eighth holds 8 x 8 = 64. You can also just add the eight odd numbers directly: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 15 = 64. The transferable idea: build the small cases and read the pattern off them, rather than guessing a formula.
solutions.elegant: The first n odd numbers always sum to n squared, because they stack into an n by n square.

problems.whyOnTest: Growth patterns are the cheapest place to practise trying small cases before reaching for a formula.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A drawer holds 12 red socks, 10 blue socks and 8 green socks, all mixed up. You take socks out one at a time in the dark. What is the smallest number of socks you must take to be certain of having three of the same colour?

choices.misconception: I thought that one more than the number of colours must give three of a kind, which only guarantees a PAIR.
I got to two of each colour, then added one more for each colour instead of one more in total.
I assumed the worst case meant emptying the largest pile of 12 reds first.
I answered with the number of socks I want rather than the number I must take to be sure of them.

hints: Ask what the unluckiest possible draw looks like.
The worst case is taking two of every colour without ever getting a third. How many socks is that?
Two of each colour is 2 x 3 = 6 socks with no colour reaching three. The seventh sock must complete a set, so the answer is 7.

solutions.reliable: Imagine the unluckiest draw possible. You could take 2 red, 2 blue and 2 green - six socks - and still have no colour three times over. So six is not enough. But there are only three colours, so the seventh sock has to be red, blue or green, and whichever it is, that colour now has three. The answer is 7. The transferable idea: to guarantee something, work out the largest number of picks that could still fail, then add one.
solutions.elegant: Two of each colour is the largest failing draw at six socks, so seven forces success.

problems.whyOnTest: Guarantee questions are answered by the worst case, never by the likely case, and that reversal is the whole skill.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the last digit of 3 multiplied by itself 2026 times, that is, of 3 to the power 2026?

choices.misconception: I used the first entry of the cycle because 2026 is even, without working out where in the cycle it lands.
I counted the cycle starting from zero, so a remainder of 2 put me one place too far along.
I assumed a power that large must end in 1.
I multiplied 3 by 2 and used the last digit of that.

hints: List the last digits of the first few powers.
3, 9, 27, 81, 243 end in 3, 9, 7, 1, 3 - the last digits repeat every four powers.
2026 divided by 4 leaves remainder 2, so 3 to the power 2026 ends like 3 squared, which is 9.

solutions.reliable: Last digits of powers always repeat. Listing them: 3^1 ends in 3, 3^2 in 9, 3^3 in 7, 3^4 in 1, and then 3^5 ends in 3 again. The cycle is 3, 9, 7, 1 and it has length 4. To find where 2026 lands, divide by 4: 2026 = 4 x 506 + 2, so the remainder is 2 and the answer matches the second entry of the cycle, which is 9. Watch the off-by-one: remainder 1 means the first entry, remainder 0 means the last. The transferable idea: every last-digit question is a cycle question, and the work is locating the exponent in the cycle.
solutions.elegant: 3^4 ends in 1, so 3^2024 ends in 1 and two more threes take it to 9.

problems.whyOnTest: Every last-digit question is really a cycle question, and the marks are lost on where the remainder lands, not on finding the cycle.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: One tap fills a tank in 6 hours. A second tap fills the same tank in 4 hours. Both taps are opened together on an empty tank. How long does it take to fill?

choices.misconception: I averaged the two times, but two taps together must be faster than either one alone.
I added the two times, which would be right for filling two tanks one after the other.
I halved the smaller of the two times, guessing that two taps must simply be twice as fast as one.
I found 2 hours 24 minutes correctly and then halved it a second time.

hints: Times do not add. Think about how much each tap does in one hour.
In one hour the first tap fills 1/6 of the tank and the second fills 1/4. Together that is 1/6 + 1/4 of a tank per hour.
1/6 + 1/4 = 5/12 of a tank per hour, so a whole tank takes 12/5 = 2.4 hours, which is 2 hours 24 minutes.

solutions.reliable: Work in rates rather than times, because rates add and times do not. In one hour the first tap fills 1/6 of the tank and the second fills 1/4, so together they fill 1/6 + 1/4 = 2/12 + 3/12 = 5/12 of the tank each hour. Filling the whole tank therefore takes 1 divided by 5/12 = 12/5 = 2.4 hours, which is 2 hours and 24 minutes. Sanity check: the answer must be less than 4 hours, the faster tap's time on its own. The transferable idea: rates add, times do not.
solutions.elegant: In 12 hours the taps would fill 2 and 3 tanks, so 5 tanks in 12 hours, which is 12/5 hours per tank.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding times instead of rates is the standard trap, and the sanity check - faster than either alone - catches it every time.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The three-digit number 4A6 is divisible by 9. What digit does A stand for?

choices.misconception: I used the divisibility test for 3 rather than the one for 9, and 4 + 2 + 6 = 12 passes it.
I checked only the last two digits, as in the test for 4, and made A6 a multiple of 9: 36.
I added 4 + 6 to get 10 and then reached for 17, thinking that was the next multiple of 9.
I put a 9 in the gap because the number is divisible by 9, so I expected a 9 to show up in it.

hints: Divisibility by 9 is a question about the digit sum.
Add the digits you already have, then ask which single digit pushes that total up to the next multiple of nine.
4 + 6 = 10. The next multiple of 9 above 10 is 18, so the missing digit is 18 - 10, and the number is 486.

solutions.reliable: A number is divisible by 9 exactly when its digits add to a multiple of 9. Here 4 + 6 = 10, so the missing digit must bring the sum to 18, giving 486. The transferable idea: a divisibility test turns a question about a whole number into a question about a small digit sum.
solutions.elegant: Only one digit from 0 to 9 can lift a sum of 10 to a multiple of nine at all, so there is nothing to test.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit-sum tests appear every year in the 3-point block, and the trap answer is always the digit that matches the divisor.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the last digit of 7 x 7 x 7 x ... x 7, where there are 20 sevens?

choices.misconception: I divided 19 by 4, got remainder 3, and took the third digit of the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 instead of moving on from 7.
I assumed the last digit of a power matches the last digit of the base, no matter the exponent.
I squared 7 to get 49 and used its last digit, ignoring the other eighteen factors.
I expected a long product to end in 0 the way multiples of ten do.

hints: Work out the first few last digits and look for a cycle.
Last digits of powers repeat. Find the length of the repeat, then divide the exponent by that length and use the remainder to pick the position.
The last digits run 7, 9, 3, then back to 7. The cycle has length 4, and 20 is a multiple of 4, so the twentieth sits at the end of a full cycle.

solutions.reliable: The last digits of successive powers of 7 are 7, 9, 3, 1 and then repeat. Since 20 is divisible by 4, the twentieth power sits at the end of a complete cycle, so the last digit is 1. The transferable idea: last digits are periodic, so an enormous exponent collapses to a remainder.
solutions.elegant: 7 x 7 x 7 x 7 ends in 1, and 20 sevens is five such blocks, so the whole product ends the same way one does.

problems.whyOnTest: Powers far beyond calculator range are standard in the middle block, and the periodic last digit is the only route that scales.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Every interior angle of a regular polygon measures 150 degrees. How many sides does it have?

choices.misconception: I divided the interior angle by the exterior angle, 150 / 30.
I used (n - 1) x 180 for the angle sum, so 150n = 180n - 180 and n = 6.
I used the exterior angle but subtracted 150 from 180 and then divided 720 rather than 360 by it.
I worked out the exterior angle, 180 - 150 = 30, and gave it as the number of sides.

hints: Exterior angles are easier here than interior ones.
Each exterior angle is 180 minus the interior angle. The exterior angles of any polygon add to 360, so divide 360 by one of them.
Each exterior angle is 180 - 150 = 30 degrees. The exterior angles total 360, and 360 / 30 gives the number of sides.

solutions.reliable: Interior and exterior angles at a vertex add to 180, so each exterior angle is 30 degrees. Every polygon's exterior angles total 360, so the polygon has 360 / 30 = 12 sides. The transferable idea: switch to exterior angles, because their total never depends on the number of sides.
solutions.elegant: Turning once round the outside of the shape is one full revolution, and each corner turns 30 degrees, so there are twelve corners.

problems.whyOnTest: The interior angle formula is the slow route and runs out of time; the exterior-angle total of 360 is the one fact that makes these instant.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A canteen offers 4 soups, 5 main courses and 3 desserts. How many different three-course meals can be chosen?

choices.misconception: I thought a meal needed every item on the menu, which is impossible, so I answered zero.
I added the numbers of choices, 4 + 5 + 3, instead of multiplying them.
I multiplied the courses I thought were the main decisions and left the soup out.
I multiplied soup by main course, 4 x 5, and forgot dessert.

hints: Each course is an independent decision.
When choices are made one after another and none restricts the next, multiply the number of options at each step rather than adding them.
There are 4 ways to pick soup, then 5 for the main, then 3 for dessert, so multiply all three.

solutions.reliable: The three courses are chosen independently, so the number of meals is 4 x 5 x 3 = 60. The transferable idea: independent decisions multiply, and the giveaway that you should multiply rather than add is the word 'and' joining the stages.

problems.whyOnTest: The multiplication principle is the single most reused counting tool on the paper, and the adding trap sits right next to it in the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Maya cycles 12 km at 18 km per hour, then walks 3 km at 6 km per hour. How many minutes is she travelling altogether?

choices.misconception: I worked out the walking time of 30 minutes and forgot to add the cycling.
I worked out the cycling time of 40 minutes and forgot to add the walk.
I added the distances and divided 15 km by the cycling speed, as if she cycled the whole way.
I averaged the two speeds to 12 km per hour and divided the total 15 km by that.

hints: Do the two legs separately before adding anything.
Time is distance divided by speed. Find each leg's time on its own, convert both into the same unit, and only then add them.
Cycling takes 12 / 18 of an hour, which is 40 minutes. Walking takes 3 / 6 of an hour, which is 30 minutes.

solutions.reliable: Cycling takes 12 / 18 hour = 40 minutes and walking takes 3 / 6 hour = 30 minutes, so the journey is 70 minutes. The transferable idea: speeds never average over unequal distances, so each leg has to be timed separately before the totals are combined.
solutions.elegant: Both legs come out as whole numbers of minutes once you notice 12 / 18 and 3 / 6 are two thirds and one half of an hour.

problems.whyOnTest: Averaging the two speeds is the most common single error in rate questions, and one distractor is built from exactly that.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 9 are written in a row. You may swap any two neighbours as often as you like. Can the row ever end up exactly reversed after an odd number of swaps?

choices.misconception: I counted the nine numbers and assumed the swap count would match them.
I guessed an odd number near the right size without checking what each swap does to the ordering.

choices.text: No, because reversing needs an even number of swaps
No, because the row can never be reversed at all
choices.misconception: I concluded that an impossible parity meant the reversal itself was impossible, rather than just the odd count.

choices.text: Only if the middle number stays put
choices.misconception: I noticed the middle number does not move and treated that as the whole constraint.

hints: Count the pairs that are in the wrong order.
Each neighbour swap changes the number of out-of-order pairs by exactly one, so that count's parity flips every move. Compare the start and the target.
Reversing 1 to 9 puts all 36 pairs out of order, and 36 is even, so the number of single swaps must be even too.

solutions.reliable: Count inversions: pairs that appear in the wrong order. A swap of neighbours changes that count by exactly one, so its parity alternates with every move. The reversed row has 9 x 8 / 2 = 36 inversions, an even number, so only an even number of swaps can reach it. The transferable idea: find a quantity whose parity every move must flip, then compare the two ends.
solutions.elegant: 36 is even, so the answer is settled before any swapping is attempted.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity invariants turn an impossible search into a one-line argument, and the 5-point block relies on them most years.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A drawer holds 10 black socks, 10 white socks and 10 grey socks, all mixed up. Reaching in without looking, how many socks must be taken to be certain of two of the same colour?

choices.misconception: I assumed the first two socks would match, which is possible but not certain.
I counted one sock for each colour and stopped, forgetting that three socks can be all different.
I used the ten socks of one colour as the worst case, as though all ten had to come out first.
I added two whole colours together, treating the worst case as emptying them.

hints: Imagine the unluckiest possible draw.
Ask what the largest number of socks is that could still avoid a match. One more than that is the answer, and the drawer's size does not matter.
Three socks could be one of each colour. A fourth sock must repeat a colour, since there are only three colours.

solutions.reliable: The worst case is one sock of each colour, which is three socks with no match. The fourth sock must repeat a colour, so four is enough and three is not. The transferable idea: pigeonhole answers are always one more than the largest collection that avoids the condition, and the number of items per colour is a distraction.
solutions.elegant: Three colours are three pigeonholes, so four socks force a shared one.

problems.whyOnTest: Pigeonhole questions dress the same argument in new clothes each year, and the quantity per category is always there to mislead.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts 5, 9, 13, 17 and keeps going up by the same amount. What is its 50th term?

choices.misconception: I multiplied 50 by the step of 4 and added the first term, counting fifty steps instead of forty-nine.
I multiplied 50 by 4 and ignored the starting value altogether.
I added 4 to 50, treating the position as if it were a term.
I counted forty-eight steps because I subtracted two from the position rather than one.

hints: The first term takes no steps to reach.
Write the rule as first term plus step times the number of steps. Getting to the nth term takes n minus one steps, not n.
The step is 4, and reaching the 50th term takes 49 steps, so it is 5 + 49 x 4.

solutions.reliable: The step is 4, and the 50th term is 49 steps past the first, so it equals 5 + 49 x 4 = 201. The transferable idea: in any arithmetic sequence the count of steps is one less than the term's position, which is where nearly every error in these comes from.
solutions.elegant: Each term is one more than a multiple of 4: the nth term is 4n + 1, so the 50th is 4 x 50 + 1.

problems.whyOnTest: The off-by-one between position and step count is the single most common sequence error, and both nearby distractors are built from it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two lighthouses flash together at midnight. One flashes every 12 seconds, the other every 18 seconds. How many seconds after midnight do they next flash together?

choices.misconception: I found the largest common factor of 12 and 18 instead of their smallest common multiple.
I added the two intervals, as though the flashes took turns.
I divided 12 x 18 = 216 by the common factor 2 instead of by the greatest common factor 6.
I multiplied 12 by 18, which is a shared moment but not the first one.

hints: List the moments each lighthouse flashes.
The shared moments are the common multiples of the two intervals, so the next one is the smallest number both intervals divide into.
Multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36. Multiples of 18 are 18, 36. The first number in both lists is the answer.

solutions.reliable: Shared flashes happen at common multiples of 12 and 18, so the next one is their lowest common multiple, 36 seconds. The transferable idea: 'next time both happen' is always a lowest common multiple, while 'largest group both split into' is a greatest common factor, and the two are routinely swapped.
solutions.elegant: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, so the smallest number carrying both is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3.

problems.whyOnTest: Factor and multiple questions hinge on which of the two is wanted, and the greatest common factor is offered as the first choice for exactly that reason.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square of side 10 cm has a square of side 6 cm cut out of one corner, with the smaller square's sides lying along the larger one's. What is the area of the shape that remains?

choices.misconception: I gave the area of the piece that was removed rather than the piece that is left.
I counted only the 10 by 4 strip of the L shape and forgot the 4 by 6 piece.
I subtracted the side lengths, 10 - 6 = 4, and squared that.
I gave the area of the original square and forgot that anything had been cut away.

hints: Find both areas first, then take one from the other.
Work out the area of the whole square and of the square removed, then subtract. Never subtract side lengths and square afterwards.
The large square is 10 x 10 = 100 and the cut-out is 6 x 6 = 36.

solutions.reliable: The large square has area 100 and the removed square has area 36, so 64 square centimetres remain. The transferable idea: areas subtract but side lengths do not, so convert every length into an area before any subtraction happens.
solutions.elegant: The remaining shape splits into a 10 by 4 strip and a 4 by 6 rectangle, which is 40 + 24.

problems.whyOnTest: Subtracting lengths and then squaring is the standard trap in shaded-area questions, and one distractor is exactly that answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A coat priced at 80 euros is reduced by 25 percent. What does it cost now?

choices.misconception: I worked out the discount of 20 euros and gave that as the price.
I subtracted 25 from 80, treating the percentage as a number of euros.
I worked out that 75 percent remains and gave 75 as the price, forgetting to take 75 percent of 80.
I added 25 percent instead of taking it off.

hints: A quarter off means three quarters remain.
Rather than finding the discount and subtracting, multiply the price by the fraction that survives. Twenty-five percent off leaves seventy-five percent.
25 percent of 80 is 20, so the new price is 80 - 20. Equivalently, three quarters of 80.

solutions.reliable: Twenty-five percent of 80 is 20, so the coat now costs 60 euros. Faster still, 25 percent off leaves three quarters, and three quarters of 80 is 60. The transferable idea: multiply by what remains rather than computing the discount and subtracting, which removes the step where the discount gets reported as the price.

problems.whyOnTest: Giving the discount instead of the new price is the most common slip in percentage questions, and it is offered as a choice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Alone, Ana paints a fence in 6 hours and Ben paints it in 12 hours. Working together at those rates, how many hours do they need?

choices.misconception: I added the rates, 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4, and gave that as the number of hours without inverting it.
I halved the faster time, assuming a second helper always doubles the speed.
I averaged 6 and 12 to get 9, as though each painted half the fence one after the other.
I added the two times, so my answer is slower than either of them working alone.

hints: Think about how much fence each paints in one hour.
Convert both times into fences per hour, add those rates, then turn the combined rate back into a time by taking its reciprocal.
Ana does one sixth an hour and Ben one twelfth, so together a quarter of the fence each hour.

solutions.reliable: In one hour Ana paints 1/6 of the fence and Ben 1/12, so together 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 each hour, and the job takes 4 hours. The transferable idea: times do not add or average, rates do, so always convert to work-per-hour first and invert at the end.
solutions.elegant: Ben is half as fast as Ana, so the two of them are like one and a half Anas, and 6 divided by 1.5 is 4.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding or averaging the times is almost universal on a first attempt, and the answer must come out faster than the quicker worker alone.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a class of 30, 18 play football and 14 play chess. Every pupil plays at least one of the two. How many play both?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 14 from 18, comparing the two clubs with each other rather than with the class.
I added the two club sizes and ignored the class total completely.
I subtracted 18 from 30 and gave the number who do not play football.
I subtracted 14 from 30 and gave the number who do not play chess.

hints: Add the two clubs and compare with the class size.
Pupils in both clubs get counted twice when the two club sizes are added, so the excess over the class total is exactly the overlap.
18 + 14 = 32, which is 2 more than 30 because the pupils in both were counted twice.

solutions.reliable: Adding the clubs gives 18 + 14 = 32, two more than the 30 pupils, and that excess is the number counted twice, so 2 play both. The transferable idea: the overlap of two sets is the amount by which their sizes overshoot the total, which is why inclusion and exclusion works.
solutions.elegant: The overshoot is the overlap, so the subtraction 32 - 30 is the whole calculation.

problems.whyOnTest: Two-set overlap questions are a fixture, and the trap is comparing the sets with each other rather than with the whole group.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Red and blue counters are in the ratio 3 to 5, and there are 64 counters altogether. How many are red?

choices.misconception: I divided 64 by the 8 parts and gave the size of one part as the answer.
I split the 64 counters in half, ignoring the ratio altogether.
I read the ratio 3 to 5 as the fraction 3/5 and took three fifths of 64.
I worked out the blue counters and gave that number instead of the red ones.

hints: Count the parts before counting the counters.
A ratio of 3 to 5 means 8 equal parts in total. Divide the total by the number of parts, then multiply by the parts belonging to the colour you want.
3 + 5 = 8 parts, so one part is 64 / 8 = 8 counters, and red has 3 parts.

solutions.reliable: The ratio has 3 + 5 = 8 parts, so each part is 64 / 8 = 8 counters and red holds 3 parts, giving 24. The transferable idea: a ratio question becomes arithmetic the moment you find the size of one part, and the usual error is answering with the part size or the wrong colour.

problems.whyOnTest: Ratio questions reward finding the part size first, and the choices include both the other colour and the bare part size.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 2 to 5. The smaller one has area 12. What is the area of the larger one?

choices.misconception: I scaled the area by the side ratio of 5 over 2, as though area grew in step with length.
I doubled twice, treating the scale factor as 2 rather than 2.5.
I multiplied the area by 5 and ignored the 2 in the ratio.
I squared the 5 and multiplied 12 by 25, forgetting to divide by 2 squared.

hints: Area does not scale the way length does.
When every length is multiplied by k, every area is multiplied by k squared. Find the length scale factor first, then square it before touching the area.
Lengths scale by 5 / 2, so areas scale by 25 / 4, and 12 x 25 / 4 is the larger area.

solutions.reliable: Lengths scale by 5/2, so areas scale by the square, 25/4. The larger area is 12 x 25 / 4 = 75. The transferable idea: a length scale factor of k multiplies areas by k squared and volumes by k cubed, and skipping the square is the error the question is built to catch.
solutions.elegant: A quarter of 12 is 3, and twenty-five of those quarters is 75.

problems.whyOnTest: Scaling area by the length ratio is the predictable mistake in similarity questions, and it is sitting there as the first choice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three friends each say one sentence. Ana: 'Ben is lying.' Ben: 'Carl is lying.' Carl: 'Ana and Ben are both lying.' How many of them are telling the truth?

choices.misconception: I assumed everybody could be lying at once, but then Carl's sentence would be true.
I let two of them be truthful without checking that their sentences then contradict each other.
I took every sentence at face value, although they accuse one another.
I gave up once the statements referred to each other, rather than testing the two cases.

hints: Test the two cases for Ana and follow each one through.
Assume Ana is truthful and work out what every other sentence must then be. Repeat assuming she is lying. Only one of the two cases survives without contradiction.
If Ana is truthful then Ben lies, so Carl is truthful, so Ana lies. That contradiction rules the case out.

solutions.reliable: Suppose Ana is truthful. Then Ben lies, so Carl is truthful, so Ana and Ben both lie, contradicting the start. So Ana lies, Ben is truthful, Carl lies, and his sentence is false because Ben is truthful. Exactly one tells the truth. The transferable idea: assume one speaker's status, propagate it, and keep the case that survives.
solutions.elegant: Ana and Ben contradict each other in every case, so exactly one of the pair is truthful, and Carl's sentence then rules out his own.

problems.whyOnTest: Self-referential statements are solved by case analysis, not by reading tone, and the 'cannot be decided' choice is there to tempt a surrender.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The mean of five numbers is 14. Four of them are 10, 12, 15 and 20. What is the fifth number?

choices.misconception: I assumed the missing number had to equal the mean itself, which only happens by coincidence.
I averaged the four numbers I was given and ignored the mean I had been told.
I gave the total of the four known numbers rather than the one that is missing.
I gave the total of all five numbers and forgot to take the four known ones away.

hints: A mean is a total in disguise.
Multiply the mean by how many numbers there are to recover the total, add up the values you were given, and subtract to find the one that is missing.
The five numbers total 5 x 14 = 70, and the four given ones total 57.

solutions.reliable: Five numbers with mean 14 total 5 x 14 = 70. The four given numbers total 57, so the fifth is 70 - 57 = 13. The transferable idea: convert a mean into a total immediately, because totals can be added and subtracted while means cannot.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning a mean into a total is the move that makes every missing-value question routine, and three distractors are intermediate numbers from that route.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Today is Tuesday. What day of the week will it be in 100 days?

choices.misconception: I assumed 100 days was a whole number of weeks, so the day would not change.
I counted Tuesday itself as the first of the two extra days, so I moved forward only one.
I worked out 14 x 7 as 97, so I moved forward three days instead of two.
I divided 100 by 7 and moved back by the remainder of 2 instead of forward.

hints: Only the remainder after dividing by seven matters.
Days of the week repeat every 7, so split the 100 days into whole weeks plus a remainder and move forward by the remainder alone.
100 = 14 x 7 + 2, so move forward two days from Tuesday.

solutions.reliable: Weeks repeat every 7 days and 100 = 14 x 7 + 2, so the whole weeks change nothing and only the 2 extra days count. Two days after Tuesday is Thursday. The transferable idea: anything that repeats with period n is governed entirely by the remainder on division by n.
solutions.elegant: 98 is a whole number of weeks, so the question is simply two days after Tuesday.

problems.whyOnTest: Cycle questions reduce to a remainder, and the common slips are counting backwards or losing the direction of travel.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers contain at least one digit 7?

choices.misconception: I counted only the numbers starting with 7 and forgot the other two positions.
I took a tenth of the 900 numbers, 90, for each of the three places and added.
I counted one hundred for each position where a 7 could sit and ignored the double counting.
I counted the numbers with no 7 at all and gave that figure instead.

hints: Counting the ones without a 7 is far easier.
When 'at least one' appears, count the cases with none of the thing and subtract from the total. Here that means choosing each digit from those that are not 7.
There are 900 three-digit numbers. Those with no 7 have 8 choices of leading digit and 9 for each of the others.

solutions.reliable: There are 900 three-digit numbers. A number with no 7 has 8 choices for the leading digit, since it cannot be 0 or 7, and 9 for each of the other two, giving 8 x 9 x 9 = 648. So 900 - 648 = 252 contain a 7. The transferable idea: 'at least one' almost always means count the complement, because the direct count double counts the numbers with two or three sevens.
solutions.elegant: Counting directly forces you to track numbers with two or three sevens; the complement has no overlaps at all.

problems.whyOnTest: Complementary counting is the difference between a clean line of arithmetic and an inclusion-exclusion mess, and the complement itself is offered as a distractor.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock at exactly 4 o'clock?

choices.misconception: I gave the size of one hour mark rather than the whole gap.
I counted three hour marks between the hands instead of four.
I counted the five numbers 12, 1, 2, 3, 4 as five gaps of 30 degrees.
I measured the angle the long way round rather than the smaller one asked for.

hints: Each hour mark is a fixed share of the full turn.
Twelve hour marks share 360 degrees, so each is worth 30. Count how many marks lie between the hands, then take the smaller of the two ways round.
At 4 o'clock the minute hand is at 12 and the hour hand at 4, which is four marks of 30 degrees.

solutions.reliable: A full turn of 360 degrees is split into 12 hour marks, so each is 30 degrees. At 4 o'clock the hands are four marks apart, giving 4 x 30 = 120 degrees, and that is already the smaller angle. The transferable idea: convert hour marks into 30-degree units first, then check which of the two angles round the dial is the smaller.
solutions.elegant: A third of the dial separates 12 and 4, and a third of 360 is 120.

problems.whyOnTest: Clock angles are routine once each mark is worth 30 degrees, and the long-way-round answer is always among the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three litres of a 20 percent salt solution are mixed with 2 litres of a 45 percent salt solution. What percentage of the mixture is salt?

choices.misconception: I averaged the two percentages and ignored that there was more of the weaker solution.
I added the two percentages together as though concentrations accumulated.
I subtracted the smaller percentage from the larger and used the difference.
I halved the stronger percentage and ignored the weaker solution completely.

hints: Work in litres of salt, not in percentages.
Find the actual amount of salt contributed by each solution, add those amounts, then divide by the total volume of the mixture. Percentages cannot be added or averaged directly.
The first brings 0.6 litres of salt and the second 0.9 litres, into 5 litres of mixture.

solutions.reliable: The first solution carries 3 x 0.20 = 0.6 litres of salt, the second 2 x 0.45 = 0.9 litres, so the mixture holds 1.5 litres of salt in 5 litres, which is 30 percent. The transferable idea: convert every percentage into an actual quantity, combine the quantities, and only convert back at the end.
solutions.elegant: The mixture is three fifths weak and two fifths strong, so the answer sits three fifths of the way from 45 down to 20.

problems.whyOnTest: A plain average of the concentrations is the standard error, and it is offered as a choice because the volumes are deliberately unequal.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the sum AB + BA = 121, the letters A and B stand for different digits. What is A + B?

choices.misconception: I found a pair of digits adding to 12 without checking the sum came to 121.
I assumed the two digits had to add to a round ten because the answer ends in one.
I read the leading 1 of 121 as the digit sum rather than a carry.
I read the last two digits of 121 as the answer to what was asked.

hints: Write each two-digit number in terms of its digits.
AB is 10A + B and BA is 10B + A. Add them and the expression collapses into a single multiple of A + B, which you can then match against 121.

solutions.reliable: AB means 10A + B and BA means 10B + A, so the sum is 11A + 11B = 11(A + B). Since 121 = 11 x 11, A + B = 11. The transferable idea: replace digit letters with place-value expressions at once, because the algebra usually collapses to something far simpler than the puzzle looks.
solutions.elegant: Reversing a two-digit number and adding always gives a multiple of 11, so 121 fixes the digit sum immediately.

problems.whyOnTest: Cryptarithms become algebra once place value is written out, and guessing digit pairs is slower and lands on the offered traps.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In how many different orders can four people stand in a queue?

choices.misconception: I multiplied four by itself, which would allow the same person to fill two positions.
I multiplied four by three and stopped before placing the last two people.
I counted the people rather than the arrangements of them.
I doubled the number of people, as though each one simply had two options.

hints: Fill the positions one at a time and count the choices left.
The first position has four candidates, the second three, and so on, because each person placed is no longer available. Multiply those shrinking counts together.
4 x 3 x 2 x 1 counts the queues, since every placement removes one person from the pool.

solutions.reliable: Fill the queue from the front: 4 choices, then 3, then 2, then 1, giving 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24. The transferable idea: arrangements multiply shrinking counts, whereas repeated independent choices multiply the same count, and confusing the two produces the 16 on offer.

problems.whyOnTest: Arrangements and repeated choices look identical in words and differ in arithmetic, so both answers sit side by side in the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Nine coins look identical but one is lighter. Using a balance that compares two groups, what is the fewest weighings that always finds the light coin?

choices.misconception: I split the coins in half each time instead of into three groups.
I weighed coins against each other one pair at a time.
I compared each coin with one known coin in turn, which is the worst possible plan.
I assumed a single weighing could separate nine coins, which it cannot.

hints: A balance has three outcomes, not two.
Split the coins into three equal groups and weigh two of them. Whichever way the balance tips, or if it does not, you are left with a group of three.
Weigh three against three. The result points at a group of three, and one more weighing of one against one finds the coin.

solutions.reliable: Weigh three coins against three. If one side rises the light coin is there; if they balance it is in the untouched three. Either way you are down to three coins, and one more weighing of one against one settles it, so two weighings suffice. The transferable idea: a balance returns one of three answers, so plan in thirds rather than in halves.
solutions.elegant: Two weighings distinguish at most nine cases, and there are exactly nine coins, so two is both achievable and unbeatable.

problems.whyOnTest: Halving is the instinct and thirding is correct, so the 3 answer that halving produces is always among the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A point is at coordinates (2, 3). It is moved 4 right and 5 down. Where does it end up?

choices.misconception: I added the downward move instead of subtracting it.
I applied the move down but left out the move to the right.
I applied the horizontal move but left the vertical one out.
I subtracted the rightward move and added the downward one, reversing both.

hints: Right adds to the first number and down subtracts from the second.
Handle the two directions separately. Moving right increases the first coordinate and moving down decreases the second, so apply one move at a time and keep the signs straight.
2 + 4 gives the first coordinate, and 3 - 5 gives the second.

solutions.reliable: Moving 4 right takes the first coordinate from 2 to 6, and moving 5 down takes the second from 3 to minus 2, giving (6, minus 2). The transferable idea: treat the two coordinates independently and let the direction fix the sign, rather than trying to picture the whole move at once.

problems.whyOnTest: Sign errors on the vertical move are the whole difficulty here, and each one-move-only answer is offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers have all three digits different and do not contain a zero?

choices.misconception: I allowed digits to repeat, using nine choices in every one of the three places.
I used ten digits for the first place, although zero is excluded throughout.
I allowed a zero in the last two places, which the question forbids.
I excluded one digit too many, leaving eight choices for every place.

hints: Count the choices for each place in turn.
Fill the places one at a time. Nine digits are available for the first, then one fewer for each later place, because digits may not repeat and zero is excluded throughout.
Nine choices, then eight, then seven.

solutions.reliable: Zero is excluded, so nine digits are available. The first place has 9 choices, the second 8 and the third 7, giving 9 x 8 x 7 = 504. The transferable idea: handle the restriction by shrinking the pool before counting, then let each placement reduce the count by one.

problems.whyOnTest: Restricted counting goes wrong when repeats slip back in, and the unrestricted counts are all offered.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence begins 7, 11, 15, 19, and continues with the same constant step. What is the 30th term?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the step by 30 instead of by 29, forgetting that the first term needs no steps.
I used 4 times 30 and forgot to add the starting value.
I added 28 steps instead of 29, counting the gaps one short.
I treated the first term as the step and used 7 times 30 minus something close.

hints: Count the gaps between terms, not the terms themselves.
Going from the 1st term to the 30th takes 29 steps of 4.

solutions.reliable: The step is 11 - 7 = 4. Reaching the 30th term from the 1st takes 29 steps, not 30, because the first term is already there before any step is taken. So the 30th term is 7 + 29 x 4 = 7 + 116 = 123. Check on a small case: the 2nd term should be 7 + 1 x 4 = 11, which matches. The transferable idea: the nth term is first + (n - 1) x step, and the minus one is where the marks go.
solutions.elegant: Every term is 3 less than a multiple of 4, so the 30th is 4 x 31 - 1 = 123.

problems.whyOnTest: The off-by-one between terms and gaps is the single most common arithmetic-sequence error.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when 2 to the power 50 is divided by 7?

choices.misconception: I assumed the cycle ends on 1 at every exponent that is a multiple of 2.
I used a remainder of 1 rather than 2 when dividing 50 by 3.
I doubled my way to 2 cubed = 8 and used 8 minus 2.
I assumed a large power of 2 must eventually be divisible by 7.

hints: Work out the remainders of the first few powers of 2 when divided by 7.
2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 leave 2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 1 - the remainders cycle with length 3.
50 divided by 3 leaves remainder 2, so 2^50 leaves the same remainder as 2^2, which is 4.

solutions.reliable: Powers repeat their remainders. Dividing by 7: 2^1 leaves 2, 2^2 leaves 4, 2^3 = 8 leaves 1, and then the pattern restarts because multiplying by 2 again gives 2. So the cycle is 2, 4, 1 with length 3. Now 50 = 3 x 16 + 2, so 2^50 sits in the same place as 2^2 and leaves remainder 4. The transferable idea: find the first exponent that returns a remainder of 1, and the cycle length is that exponent.
solutions.elegant: 2^3 leaves 1, so 2^48 leaves 1, and two more doublings give 4.

problems.whyOnTest: Modular cycles turn an impossible calculation into a division you can do in your head.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two towns are 300 km apart. A car leaves each town at the same moment driving toward the other, one at 60 km/h and the other at 90 km/h. How long until they meet?

choices.misconception: I used only the slower car's speed and divided 300 by 90 the wrong way round.
I averaged the two speeds to 75 km/h and divided 300 by it, which ignores that both cars move at once.
I divided 300 by 60, using only the slower car.
I halved the distance to 150 and then divided by 150, applying the closing speed twice.

hints: The gap closes from both ends at once.
Every hour the gap closes by 60 + 90 = 150 km.

solutions.reliable: When two objects move toward each other, the distance between them closes at the sum of their speeds. Here the gap shrinks by 60 + 90 = 150 km every hour, so a 300 km gap closes in 300 / 150 = 2 hours. Check it directly: in 2 hours the first car covers 120 km and the second covers 180 km, and 120 + 180 = 300. The transferable idea: approaching speeds add, receding speeds also add, and same-direction speeds subtract.
solutions.elegant: In two hours the cars cover 120 and 180 km, and those already fill the 300 km road.

problems.whyOnTest: Closing speed is the one idea that turns most two-object motion problems into a single division.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A club has 8 members. In how many ways can a group of 3 be chosen to attend a conference, if the three places are all the same?

choices.misconception: I counted ordered selections, so I counted the same three people once for every order they could stand in.
I multiplied the 8 members by the 3 places, which counts something quite different from a selection.
I divided the 336 ordered selections by 3 instead of by 3 factorial.
I chose 2 people rather than 3.

hints: The three places are identical.
There are 8 x 7 x 6 = 336 ways to pick three people in order. Each group of three has been counted several times.
Each group of 3 appears 3! = 6 times in that list, so the answer is 336 / 6 = 56.

solutions.reliable: Count the ordered picks first, then correct for the overcounting. Choosing three people in order gives 8 x 7 x 6 = 336 possibilities. But the places are identical, so a group like {Ana, Ben, Cara} has been counted once for each of the 3! = 6 orders those three could be named in. Dividing gives 336 / 6 = 56. The transferable idea: when order does not matter, count as if it did and then divide by the number of orderings.
solutions.elegant: This is 8 choose 3, which is (8 x 7 x 6) / (3 x 2 x 1) = 56.

problems.whyOnTest: Overcount-then-correct is the workhorse of every selection question, and dividing by the wrong number is the usual slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two triangles are similar. The sides of the smaller are 3/5 as long as the matching sides of the larger. The smaller triangle has area 18 square cm. What is the area of the larger triangle?

choices.misconception: I scaled the area by 5/3, using the side ratio directly instead of its square.
I multiplied the area by 2.5, halfway between the side ratio and its square.
I scaled by 3/5 instead of 5/3, making the larger triangle smaller.
I multiplied by 5 and ignored the 3 in the ratio entirely.

hints: Area does not scale the same way length does.
If every length is multiplied by k, the area is multiplied by k squared.
The larger sides are 5/3 of the smaller, so its area is (5/3) squared = 25/9 times as big: 18 x 25/9 = 50.

solutions.reliable: Under a scale factor k, every length multiplies by k but area multiplies by k squared, because area is a product of two lengths. Going from the smaller triangle to the larger multiplies lengths by 5/3, so it multiplies area by (5/3)^2 = 25/9. The larger area is therefore 18 x 25/9 = 50 square cm. Sanity check the direction: the larger triangle must have the larger area, which rules out anything below 18. The transferable idea: lengths scale by k and areas by k squared, because an area is a product of two lengths.
solutions.elegant: Areas of similar figures are in the ratio 9 to 25, and 18 is 9 x 2, so the larger is 25 x 2 = 50.

problems.whyOnTest: Scaling area by the length factor rather than its square is one of the most reliably examined mistakes in geometry.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four litres of a solution that is 25 percent acid are mixed with six litres of a solution that is 50 percent acid. What percentage of the mixture is acid?

choices.misconception: I averaged 25 and 50 without weighting by how much of each solution there was.
I added the two percentages together, which cannot be right because a mixture can never be stronger than its strongest ingredient.
I weighted the percentages by the wrong volumes, giving the 25 percent solution the larger share.
I used only the acid from the weaker solution and spread it over all ten litres.

hints: Percentages only average when the amounts match.
Work out how many litres of pure acid are in each solution, then add them.
0.25 x 4 = 1 litre and 0.50 x 6 = 3 litres, so 4 litres of acid in 10 litres of mixture, which is 40 percent.

solutions.reliable: Track the acid itself rather than the percentages. The first solution contributes 0.25 x 4 = 1 litre of acid; the second contributes 0.50 x 6 = 3 litres. Together that is 4 litres of acid in 4 + 6 = 10 litres of mixture, so the concentration is 4/10 = 40 percent. The transferable idea: a weighted average always lands nearer the ingredient you used more of - here nearer 50 than 25, which a plain average of 37.5 would miss.
solutions.elegant: There is more of the strong solution, so the answer must exceed the midpoint of 37.5, and only 40 does.

problems.whyOnTest: The plain average is the trap, and noticing which side the answer must fall on eliminates it before any arithmetic.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six friends sit around a circular table. Two seatings count as the same if one can be turned into the other by rotating the table. How many genuinely different seatings are there?

choices.misconception: I counted every arrangement in a row, so each circular seating got counted once for every rotation.
I divided 720 by 20 or some other number instead of by the 6 rotations.
I divided by 12, treating reflections as identical too, though the question only allows rotations.
I fixed two people rather than one, dividing by an extra factor.

hints: Rotating a circular seating does not change who is next to whom.
There are 6! = 720 ways to seat six people in labelled chairs. Each circular seating appears once for every rotation of the table.
There are 6 rotations, so the answer is 720 / 6 = 120.

solutions.reliable: Start by pretending the chairs are labelled: that gives 6! = 720 arrangements. But turning the table produces a seating that the question calls the same, and there are 6 rotations of a six-seat table, so every genuinely different seating has been counted 6 times. Dividing gives 720 / 6 = 120. An equivalent and often faster route: seat one person first to kill the rotation, then arrange the remaining five in 5! = 120 ways. The transferable idea: to count up to a symmetry, either divide by the number of symmetries or fix one object to remove them.
solutions.elegant: Fix one friend's seat to remove the rotations, then the other five can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting up to symmetry is exactly where a correct count becomes a wrong answer, and fixing one object is the cleanest fix.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 10 are written on a board. You repeatedly rub out any two of them and write down their positive difference instead, until a single number is left. What can be said about that final number?

choices.misconception: I checked the parity of the count of numbers rather than of their sum.

choices.text: It can be either odd or even
choices.misconception: I tried two examples, got different answers, and concluded nothing is forced.
I assumed differences must shrink all the way to nothing.
I found one sequence of moves ending at 1 and assumed every sequence must.

hints: Look for something about the whole board that never changes when you make a move.
Replacing a and b by their difference changes the total by a + b - |a - b|, which is always an even amount.
The starting sum 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55 is odd, and every move changes the sum by an even number, so the final single number is odd.

solutions.reliable: Track the parity of the total. The starting sum is 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55, which is odd. A move replaces a and b by |a - b|, so the sum drops by a + b - |a - b|, which equals 2b or 2a - either way, an even number. Since the sum starts odd and only ever changes by an even amount, it stays odd forever. At the end one number remains and it IS the sum, so that number is odd. The transferable idea: when a process looks chaotic, look for a quantity it cannot change.
solutions.elegant: Differences preserve parity, so the whole board's parity is locked to the parity of 55 from the first move to the last.

problems.whyOnTest: An invariant turns a question with countless possible move orders into a single observation about parity.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: An ordinary six-sided die is rolled three times. What is the probability that at least one roll shows a six?

choices.misconception: I added 1/6 three times, which counts the overlapping cases more than once and would exceed 1 for seven rolls.
I worked out the probability of NO six and forgot to subtract it from 1.
I found the probability of three sixes instead of at least one.
I gave the probability for a single roll and ignored that there are three.

hints: At least one is much easier to count by asking about the opposite.
The opposite of at least one six is no sixes at all in three rolls.
Each roll avoids a six with probability 5/6, so no sixes has probability (5/6)^3 = 125/216, and the answer is 1 - 125/216 = 91/216.

solutions.reliable: The phrase at least one is a signal to count the complement. The opposite event is no six on any of the three rolls. Each roll avoids a six with probability 5/6, and the rolls are independent, so no sixes has probability (5/6)^3 = 125/216. The event we want is everything else: 1 - 125/216 = 91/216, which is a little over 42 percent. The transferable idea: at least one almost always means one minus none.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding 1/6 three times is the classic error, and it visibly breaks at seven rolls where it would give a probability above 1.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when 2 to the power 100 is divided by 7?

choices.misconception: I worked out the last digit of the power first and then divided that by 7.
I found the cycle 2, 4, 1 but used a remainder of 2 where dividing 100 by 3 gives 1.
I found that the remainders repeat every 3 steps and gave the cycle length, 3, as the remainder.
I treated 100 as a multiple of the cycle length 3 and took the value at the end of the cycle.

hints: Work out the first few remainders and watch for a repeat.
Powers of a fixed base leave remainders that cycle. Find the cycle length, divide the exponent by it, and read off the position the remainder points to.
The remainders run 2, 4, 1 and then repeat, so the cycle has length 3. Since 100 = 33 x 3 + 1, the answer sits at the first position.

solutions.reliable: Powers of 2 leave remainders 2, 4, 1 on division by 7, repeating with period 3. Because 100 leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, the hundredth power sits at the first position in the cycle. The transferable idea: modular arithmetic turns an unreachable exponent into a remainder on a tiny cycle length.
solutions.elegant: 2 cubed is 8, which is one more than 7, so 2 to the 99 behaves like 1 and only one factor of 2 is left over.

problems.whyOnTest: Exponents far beyond any calculator are standard in the 4-point block, and the cycle length is what a student must find rather than recall.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A club has 8 members. How many different three-member committees can be formed?

choices.misconception: I counted the ordered selections and never divided out the orderings of a committee.
I divided the ordered count by 3 rather than by the 6 ways to order three people.
I multiplied 8 by 3, treating this as a single pass through the membership.
I added the two numbers in the question instead of combining the choices.

hints: Order does not matter inside a committee.
First count the selections as if order mattered, then divide by the number of ways the chosen people could have been ordered, because each committee was counted that many times.
8 x 7 x 6 = 336 counts ordered picks, and each committee of three appears 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 times.

solutions.reliable: Picking in order gives 8 x 7 x 6 = 336, but each committee of three has been counted in all 6 of its orders, so the answer is 336 / 6 = 56. The transferable idea: overcount deliberately, then divide by the exact size of the overcount, which is safer than trying to count unordered objects directly.
solutions.elegant: Choosing three to include is the same as choosing five to leave out, and the smaller calculation is the same number.

problems.whyOnTest: Selections and arrangements differ only by the division at the end, and the undivided count is always offered as a choice.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A board shows the numbers 1 to 10. You may erase any two and write their positive difference. Repeating until one number remains, which values are possible for that last number?

choices.misconception: I assumed every total was reachable because the moves look unrestricted.
I gave the sum of 1 to 10, which is the starting total rather than anything reachable.
I checked one example, found an even result, and generalised from the single case.
I assumed the process always drives the board down to the smallest positive value.

hints: Watch what each move does to the parity of the total.
Replacing two numbers by their difference changes the sum by twice the smaller one, so the sum's parity never changes. Work out the parity of the starting sum.
1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55, which is odd, and every move leaves the parity of the sum untouched.

solutions.reliable: Replacing a and b by their difference reduces the sum by 2 times the smaller, so the sum's parity is invariant. The starting sum 55 is odd, so the final single number is odd. Every odd value from 1 to 9 is reachable. The transferable idea: when moves look unconstrained, look for a quantity they cannot change, and parity of a sum is the first one to try.
solutions.elegant: 55 is odd, and no move can change that, so the answer needs no search at all.

problems.whyOnTest: Invariant questions are the backbone of the 5-point block, and the distractors are all results of trying examples instead of finding the invariant.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A car drives 60 km at 60 km per hour and returns the same 60 km at 30 km per hour. What is its average speed for the whole trip?

choices.misconception: I divided 60 km by the 3 hours, forgetting the trip there and back is 120 km.
I gave the slower speed, assuming the slow leg governs the whole journey.
I averaged the two speeds, which would only be right if equal times were spent at each.
I weighted the speeds 2 to 1 the wrong way round, giving the faster speed the bigger share: (2 x 60 + 30) / 3 = 50.

hints: Average speed is total distance over total time.
Do not touch the two speeds directly. Work out the time for each leg, add them, and divide the whole distance by that total time.
The outward leg takes 1 hour and the return leg 2 hours, for 120 km in 3 hours.

solutions.reliable: The outward leg takes 60 / 60 = 1 hour and the return 60 / 30 = 2 hours, so 120 km takes 3 hours and the average speed is 40 km per hour. The transferable idea: average speed is always total distance over total time, and the plain mean of two speeds is correct only when the times, not the distances, are equal.
solutions.elegant: Twice as long is spent at the slower speed, so the answer must sit nearer 30 than 60, which rules out the mean immediately.

problems.whyOnTest: The average of the two speeds is the answer almost everybody writes first, and it is deliberately on offer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A price rises by 20 percent and then falls by 20 percent. Compared with the original, the final price is

choices.misconception: I applied only the rise and forgot that a fall followed it.
I cancelled the two 20 percents, forgetting that the fall acts on the larger price.
I got the size of the change right but the direction wrong.
I added the two percentages together and treated the result as a single fall.

hints: The fall is taken from a larger amount than the rise was.
Follow a convenient starting price such as 100 through both steps, multiplying rather than adding percentages. Compare the end value with the start.
100 becomes 120, and 20 percent of 120 is 24, so the price lands at 96.

solutions.reliable: Start at 100. A 20 percent rise gives 120, and a 20 percent fall from 120 removes 24, landing at 96, which is 4 percent below the start. The transferable idea: percentage changes multiply rather than add, so a rise and an equal fall never cancel, and the order of the two does not matter.
solutions.elegant: 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96 settles it in one line, and the same product appears whichever change comes first.

problems.whyOnTest: Believing that an equal rise and fall cancel is one of the most durable errors in percentage work, and it is the second choice here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence has first term 1, second term 2, and every later term is the sum of the two before it. How many of the first twelve terms are even?

choices.misconception: I wrote out only the first six terms and found two even ones.
I counted terms 5, 8 and 11 as the even ones but missed the given second term, 2.
I assumed the terms alternated between odd and even all the way along.
I counted the odd terms by mistake and reported that total instead.

hints: Track only whether each term is odd or even.
Replace every term by the word odd or even and apply the rule to those labels alone. The labels fall into a short repeating block, which you can then count across twelve positions.
The parities run odd, even, odd, odd, even, odd, and then repeat every three terms.

solutions.reliable: Keeping only parity, the rule odd plus even is odd, and so on, produces the repeating block odd, even, odd. Over twelve terms that block appears four times, so four terms are even. The transferable idea: when a recursion is only being asked about parity, work entirely in parities and the problem collapses to a cycle of length three.
solutions.elegant: Every third term is the even one, so twelve terms contain exactly twelve divided by three of them.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive sequences grow too fast to write out at contest length, and reducing the recursion to parity is the move that makes it finishable.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two cubes have edges in the ratio 1 to 3. How many of the smaller cube fit inside the larger one?

choices.misconception: I used the edge ratio directly, as though volume grew in step with length.
I squared the ratio, which would compare surface areas rather than volumes.
I doubled the squared ratio in a half-remembered attempt at the volume rule.
I raised the ratio to the fourth power, going one step past the three dimensions.

hints: Count how the ratio acts along each of three directions.
A length scale factor acts once for each dimension, so volume is multiplied by the factor cubed. Work out the factor from the edges first.
The edges scale by 3, so volumes scale by 3 x 3 x 3.

solutions.reliable: Scaling every edge by 3 multiplies the volume by 3 cubed, so 27 small cubes fill the large one. The transferable idea: a length factor of k multiplies areas by k squared and volumes by k cubed, because it acts once per dimension.
solutions.elegant: The large cube is a 3 by 3 by 3 stack of small ones, which can simply be counted.

problems.whyOnTest: Squaring instead of cubing is the standard scaling error, and both the squared and the unscaled answers are on offer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A token moves along the grid lines of a 3 by 3 square of cells, one unit right or one unit up at a time, from the bottom-left corner point to the top-right corner point. How many different routes are there?

choices.misconception: I counted the six steps in a single route instead of the number of different routes.
I multiplied the three rights by the three ups, which is not how a route is built.
I squared the six steps, double counting every route many times over.
I gave two choices at each of six steps, ignoring that the counts of rights and ups are fixed.

hints: Every route uses the same number of steps.
A route is three rights and three ups in some order, so counting routes means counting which of the six steps are the rights. That is a selection, not a product.
Choose which three of the six steps are rights: 6 x 5 x 4 divided by 3 x 2 x 1.

solutions.reliable: Every route is a sequence of three rights and three ups, so a route is fixed by choosing which three of the six steps are rights, giving 6 x 5 x 4 / 6 = 20. The transferable idea: a lattice path is a word in two letters, so counting paths is counting positions, which is a selection.
solutions.elegant: Writing the running totals into the grid gives Pascal's triangle, and the far corner holds the answer directly.

problems.whyOnTest: Grid paths recur every few years, and the product of the two step counts is the plausible wrong answer sitting right there.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Adding one more number to a list of nine numbers raises the mean from 12 to 13. What number was added?

choices.misconception: I assumed the new number had to equal the new mean.
I added the rise of 1 to the new mean, 13 + 1, forgetting that each of the other nine numbers needed lifting too.
I added nine to the old mean, mixing up the count with the rise.
I gave the new total rather than the number that produced it.

hints: Compare the two totals rather than the two means.
Turn each mean into a total: nine numbers at 12, then ten numbers at 13. The difference between those totals is the number that was added.
Nine numbers at mean 12 total 108, and ten at mean 13 total 130.

solutions.reliable: Nine numbers with mean 12 total 108, and ten with mean 13 total 130, so the number added is 130 - 108 = 22. The transferable idea: means never subtract usefully but totals do, so convert to totals before comparing anything.
solutions.elegant: The newcomer must be the new mean plus the 1 it lifted each of the nine others, which is 13 + 9.

problems.whyOnTest: Changing-mean questions are routine once both means become totals, and the tempting answers are the new mean itself and the new total.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two circles of radius 5 touch each other on the outside. A third circle of radius 5 touches both. What is the perimeter of the triangle joining the three centres?

choices.misconception: I used the three radii as the side lengths of the triangle.
I added a diameter to two radii, mixing the two measurements.
I took each side as a diameter plus a radius, 15, and tripled it.
I measured each side from the far edge of one circle to the far edge of the other, 20, and tripled it.

hints: The distance between centres of touching circles is a sum of radii.
Two circles that touch on the outside have centres exactly the sum of their radii apart. Work out one side that way, then use the symmetry of the arrangement.
Each side joins two centres, so each is 5 + 5 = 10, and the triangle is equilateral.

solutions.reliable: When two circles touch externally the distance between centres equals the sum of the radii, here 5 + 5 = 10. All three sides are 10, so the perimeter is 30. The transferable idea: in touching-circle problems, replace every contact with the centre-to-centre distance and the picture becomes a plain polygon.
solutions.elegant: The three centres form an equilateral triangle of side one diameter, so the perimeter is three diameters.

problems.whyOnTest: Converting tangency into centre distances is the whole technique, and the radius-only and edge-to-edge answers are both on offer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two opposite corner squares are removed from an 8 by 8 chessboard. Can the remaining 62 squares be covered exactly by 31 dominoes, each covering two squares?

choices.text: Yes, and there are many ways
choices.misconception: I checked that 62 is twice 31 and assumed the count was the only obstacle.
I assumed a tight fit meant a unique arrangement rather than none at all.

choices.text: Only if the dominoes may overlap
choices.misconception: I looked for a way to relax the rules instead of testing whether the colours allow it.

choices.text: No, because the two removed squares share a colour
No, because 62 is not divisible by 2
choices.misconception: I claimed a divisibility obstacle that does not exist, since 62 is even.

hints: Colour the board and count what a domino must cover.
Every domino covers one square of each colour, so any covered region needs equal numbers of the two colours. Check the colours of the squares that were removed.
Opposite corners are the same colour, so the board is left with 32 of one colour and 30 of the other.

solutions.reliable: Each domino covers exactly one dark and one light square, so a fully covered region must hold equal numbers of each. Opposite corners share a colour, so removing them leaves 32 of one and 30 of the other, and no covering exists. The transferable idea: a colouring gives a quantity every piece must respect, which proves impossibility without any searching.
solutions.elegant: 31 dominoes cover 31 of each colour, and 30 is not 31.

problems.whyOnTest: Colouring arguments prove impossibility in one line where a search would take the whole paper, and the counting-only answer is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Roughly how many seconds are there in a year?

choices.misconception: I converted the year into minutes, 365 x 24 x 60, and stopped one step short of seconds.
I used 360 seconds in an hour instead of 3600.
I used 3650 days in a year, slipping a factor of ten into the day count.
I multiplied by 60 one time too many, as though there were another sixty-step unit below the second.

hints: Build the answer one conversion at a time.
Go from a year to days, days to hours, hours to minutes and minutes to seconds, checking after each step that the size of the number has grown by about the right factor.
365 x 24 is about 8800 hours, times 3600 seconds in an hour.

solutions.reliable: A year is about 365 x 24 = 8760 hours, and each hour holds 3600 seconds, giving roughly 31.5 million. The transferable idea: estimate one conversion at a time and sanity-check the order of magnitude after each, because a single missed factor of sixty moves the answer by a whole choice.
solutions.elegant: A useful fact worth carrying: a year is close to pi times ten million seconds.

problems.whyOnTest: Order-of-magnitude questions are won by the student who tracks powers of ten, and every distractor here is one conversion away from right.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a group of 40 people, 25 speak French, 20 speak German and 8 speak neither. How many speak both?

choices.misconception: I compared 25 + 20 with the whole group of 40 and forgot to remove the 8 who speak neither.
I reused the number who speak neither as though it were the overlap.
I found the number who speak at least one language and stopped there.
I added the two language counts and ignored both the group size and the eight.

hints: Set aside the people who speak neither first.
Take the eight away from the group to find how many speak at least one language, then compare that with the sum of the two language counts. The excess is the overlap.
40 - 8 = 32 speak at least one, while 25 + 20 = 45 counts the bilingual people twice.

solutions.reliable: Removing the 8 leaves 32 speaking at least one language, while 25 + 20 = 45 counts the bilingual people twice, so the overlap is 45 - 32 = 13. The transferable idea: handle the 'neither' group before anything else, so the inclusion and exclusion step compares two totals that describe the same people.
